# Cloud Armor Method Enforcement HTTP Methods

Based on the forum discussion, the specific HTTP methods allowed or blocked by the methodenforcement rule are not explicitly listed in the provided content.

## What We Know

The discussion centers on a limitation: the `owasp-crs-v030301-id911100-methodenforcement` rule "is triggering on HTTP methods our system requires." While the OWASP CRS ruleset itself supports configuration to add additional methods, **Cloud Armor does not expose this functionality**.

## Workaround for REST APIs

Since modifying the CRS configuration isn't supported in Cloud Armor, the suggested solution is creating custom WAF rules. For example, to allow PATCH requests to specific endpoints:

```
gcloud compute security-policies rules create 1000 \
--security-policy my-security-policy \
--expression "request.method == 'PATCH' && request.url.path == '/my-api/resource'" \
--action allow
```

You can craft similar expressions for PUT and DELETE methods on your specific URLs or IP ranges rather than relying on the preconfigured enforcement rule.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about the Cloud Armor WAF 8 KB body inspection limit bypass vulnerability:

## Overview

Cloud Armor only inspects the first 8192 bytes (8 KB) of incoming HTTP POST request bodies. The default behaviour for Cloud Armor when a request exceeds the 8 KB limitation—specifically, when a payload that would otherwise be blocked is included after the first 8192 bytes of an HTTP POST request body—is to let the request pass directly to the underlying web application.

## Exploitation Method

This issue can be exploited by crafting an HTTP POST request with a body size exceeding the 8 KB size limitation of Cloud Armor, where the payload appears after the 8192th byte/character in the request body. An attacker could craft an HTTP PUT or PATCH request with a malicious payload in the request body to bypass the WAF without having to append 8192 bytes of padding to the payload.

## Security Impact

This may result in weaknesses in the underlying web application to be exposed to attackers and can lead to compromise of the underlying web application.

## Mitigation

A Cloud Armor rule to filter and block requests where the value of the Content-Length HTTP request header exceeds 8192 bytes can be used to mitigate the impact of the bypass. A rule that would allow requests larger than 8 KB only for a specific endpoint could be added to the security policy targeting a given application.

# Cloud Armor Request Logging Guide

## Enabling Logging

Request logging is **disabled by default** for new backend services. You must manually enable it to record Cloud Armor logs. For external Application Load Balancers, enable logging through the Global external ALB logging page. For external proxy Network Load Balancers, use Google Cloud CLI commands—console enablement isn't available.

## Key Log Fields for WAF Rules

The `enforcedSecurityPolicy` section contains critical identifiers:

- **`name`**: The security policy name
- **`priority`**: Numerical priority of the matching rule
- **`preconfiguredExprIds`**: "the IDs of all preconfigured WAF rule expressions that triggered the rule"
- **`configuredAction`**: The action type (ALLOW, DENY, THROTTLE, etc.)

## Preview vs. Enforce Mode Logging

Both modes appear in logs but serve different purposes:

- **Enforce mode** (`enforcedSecurityPolicy`): Documents rules actively blocking/allowing traffic
- **Preview mode** (`previewSecurityPolicy`): Populated only "when a preview rule would have taken priority over the enforced rule," allowing you to test rule changes without impact

## Querying for WAF Violations

Use Logs Explorer filters like:

- `jsonPayload.statusDetails="denied_by_security_policy"` for denied requests
- `jsonPayload.enforcedSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"` for specific denial outcomes

These filters help identify which requests triggered security rules and their outcomes.

# Architecture Research

**Domain:** Cross-project Cloud Armor WAF centralization for multi-project GCP infrastructure
**Researched:** 2026-02-24
**Confidence:** HIGH (GCP behavior verified via official docs; Terraform patterns verified via provider docs and community)

## Critical Finding: Cross-Project Policy Sharing Is Not Possible

Cloud Armor `google_compute_security_policy` is a project-scoped global resource. A security policy created in `security-454414` (sec workspace) **cannot be directly attached** to a backend service in `qa-apps-454414`, `prod-apps-454414`, `liftit-bi`, or `shared-016`. The `cloud_armor_policy` parameter of `google_compute_backend_service` only accepts policies owned by the same project as the backend service.

This means the originally stated goal — "single centralized policy in sec project, referenced cross-project by all LBs" — is architecturally invalid and will fail at the GCP API level.

**Source:** GCP Cloud Armor documentation (per-project quotas, policy-to-backend-service attachment scoped to same project). Verified via [Configure Cloud Armor security policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/configure-security-policies) and [Quotas and limits](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/quotas). Confidence: HIGH.

The viable centralized strategy is: **one Terraform module (sec/waf) deploys identical policies into every target project using multi-project providers**, with the WAF policy self_link output used by each LB module via remote state.

---

## System Overview

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         sec/waf Module                              │
│         (Terraform workspace: sec, run once, manages all)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  provider "google" { alias = "qa"   project = "qa-apps-454414"  }  │
│  provider "google" { alias = "prod" project = "prod-apps-454414"}  │
│  provider "google" { alias = "sha"  project = "shared-016"      }  │
│  provider "google" { alias = "bi"   project = "liftit-bi"       }  │
│  provider "google" { alias = "sec"  project = "security-454414" }  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  module "waf_qa"   { source = tf-modules//waf  provider = qa   }   │
│  module "waf_prod" { source = tf-modules//waf  provider = prod }   │
│  module "waf_sha"  { source = tf-modules//waf  provider = sha  }   │
│  module "waf_bi"   { source = tf-modules//waf  provider = bi   }   │
└────────┬────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────-─┘
         │ outputs:           │ outputs:
         │ qa_policy_self_link│ prod_policy_self_link...
         ▼                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Terraform Remote State                           │
│              bucket: liftit-tf-state / prefix: sec/waf             │
│           workspace: sec (single state for all deployments)        │
└────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │ data "terraform_remote_state" "waf" { workspace = "sec" }
         │
  ┌──────┴──────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                         │
  ▼                                         ▼
┌─────────────────────┐         ┌───────────────────────┐
│  apps/gke (qa ws)   │         │  apps/gke (prod ws)   │
│  apps/frontends     │         │  apps/frontends       │
│  apps/airflow       │         │  apps/airflow         │
│  apps/apps          │         │  apps/apps            │
│                     │         │                       │
│  cloud_armor_policy │         │  cloud_armor_policy   │
│  = remote_state     │         │  = remote_state       │
│    .waf.outputs     │         │    .waf.outputs       │
│    .qa_policy_link  │         │    .prod_policy_link  │
└─────────────────────┘         └───────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────┐         ┌───────────────────────┐
│  common/apps (sha)  │         │  bi/apps (bi ws)      │
│                     │         │  bi/wrenai-poc        │
│  cloud_armor_policy │         │                       │
│  = sha_policy_link  │         │  cloud_armor_policy   │
└─────────────────────┘         │  = bi_policy_link     │
                                └───────────────────────┘
```

## Component Responsibilities

| Component | Responsibility | Current State | Target State |
|-----------|----------------|---------------|--------------|
| `sec/waf` | WAF policy definitions — rules, priorities, rate limits, IP whitelist | Deploys one policy per workspace (qa/staging/prod/sha/sec) | Deploys policies per target project from single run using multi-provider |
| `tf-modules//waf` | Creates `google_compute_security_policy` + `google_compute_security_policy_rule` | Unchanged | Unchanged — module stays as-is |
| `tf-modules//load-balancer` | Accepts `cloud_armor_policy` string (self_link or name) | `null` | Receives self_link from remote state |
| `apps/gke`, `apps/frontends`, `apps/airflow`, `apps/apps`, `common/apps`, `bi/apps`, `bi/wrenai-poc` | Attach WAF policy to their LB backend services | `cloud_armor_policy = null` | `cloud_armor_policy = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.{env}_policy_self_link` |

## Recommended Module Structure

```
sec/waf/
├── backend.tf          # GCS state: liftit-tf-state / prefix sec/waf
├── versions.tf         # Terraform ~> 1.14, Google ~> 7.0 (NO workspace strategy change needed)
├── providers.tf        # NEW: multi-alias providers for qa/prod/sha/bi/sec projects
├── locals.tf           # IP whitelist per env, rule definitions
├── remote-state.tf     # folders, dns (unchanged)
├── waf.tf              # CHANGED: one waf module call per target project, each with provider alias
├── outputs.tf          # CHANGED: export self_link per project (qa_policy_self_link, etc.)
└── CLAUDE.md

# Consumer modules add to remote-state.tf:
data "terraform_remote_state" "waf" {
  backend   = "gcs"
  workspace = "sec"
  config = {
    bucket = "liftit-tf-state"
    prefix = "sec/waf"
  }
}
```

## Architectural Patterns

### Pattern 1: Multi-Provider in sec/waf (NEW)

**What:** Deploy identical WAF policies across multiple GCP projects from a single Terraform state using provider aliases.

**When to use:** When a resource cannot be shared cross-project (like Cloud Armor policies) but must maintain identical configuration. Eliminates per-workspace deploys.

**Trade-offs:** Single state file manages all WAF policies — simpler rule management, but a bug in `waf.tf` affects all projects simultaneously. Requires Terraform SA in sec to have `compute.securityPolicies.*` in every target project.

**Example:**

```hcl
# sec/waf/providers.tf
provider "google" {
  alias   = "qa"
  project = "qa-apps-454414"
}

provider "google" {
  alias   = "prod"
  project = "prod-apps-454414"
}

provider "google" {
  alias   = "sha"
  project = "shared-016"
}

provider "google" {
  alias   = "bi"
  project = "liftit-bi"
}

# sec/waf/waf.tf
module "waf_qa" {
  source             = "git::ssh://git@github.com/liftitapp/tf-modules.git//waf"
  providers          = { google = google.qa }
  policy_name        = "liftit-waf-qa"
  policy_description = "Politica de seguridad WAF Liftit - QA"
  rules              = local.waf_rules_qa  # shared base + qa-specific exclusions
}

module "waf_prod" {
  source             = "git::ssh://git@github.com/liftitapp/tf-modules.git//waf"
  providers          = { google = google.prod }
  policy_name        = "liftit-waf-prod"
  policy_description = "Politica de seguridad WAF Liftit - Prod"
  rules              = local.waf_rules_prod  # same base rules, potentially different exclusions
}

module "waf_sha" {
  source             = "git::ssh://git@github.com/liftitapp/tf-modules.git//waf"
  providers          = { google = google.sha }
  policy_name        = "liftit-waf-sha"
  policy_description = "Politica de seguridad WAF Liftit - SHA"
  rules              = local.waf_rules_base
}

module "waf_bi" {
  source             = "git::ssh://git@github.com/liftitapp/tf-modules.git//waf"
  providers          = { google = google.bi }
  policy_name        = "liftit-waf-bi"
  policy_description = "Politica de seguridad WAF Liftit - BI"
  rules              = local.waf_rules_bi  # exclude superset/metabase SQLi paths
}
```

### Pattern 2: Remote State Output Propagation (EXISTING, EXTENDED)

**What:** Consumer modules read WAF policy self_links from `sec/waf` remote state and pass them to the load balancer module.

**When to use:** This is the existing Liftit remote state pattern — already used for KMS keys, VPC IDs, SSL certs. Extending it to WAF policy outputs is consistent with the codebase.

**Trade-offs:** Creates a hard dependency — LB modules cannot apply until `sec/waf` has been applied first. This is acceptable because `sec/waf` is a Layer 2 resource and LBs are Layer 5.

**Example:**

```hcl
# In apps/gke/remote-state.tf (ADD)
data "terraform_remote_state" "waf" {
  backend   = "gcs"
  workspace = "sec"
  config = {
    bucket = "liftit-tf-state"
    prefix = "sec/waf"
  }
}

# In apps/gke/load-balancer.tf (CHANGE)
module "gke-apps-load-balancer" {
  source             = "git::ssh://git@github.com/liftitapp/tf-modules.git//load-balancer"
  # ... existing params ...
  cloud_armor_policy = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.qa_policy_self_link
  # For prod workspace: .outputs.prod_policy_self_link
}
```

```hcl
# sec/waf/outputs.tf (REPLACE current outputs)
output "qa_policy_self_link" {
  value = module.waf_qa.policy_self_link
}

output "prod_policy_self_link" {
  value = module.waf_prod.policy_self_link
}

output "sha_policy_self_link" {
  value = module.waf_sha.policy_self_link
}

output "bi_policy_self_link" {
  value = module.waf_bi.policy_self_link
}
```

### Pattern 3: Per-Environment WAF Rule Exclusions via Locals (NEW)

**What:** Store WAF rule sets as Terraform locals in `sec/waf/locals.tf`. A base rule set is shared across all environments. High-risk services get additional `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusions added to the rule map for their environment's policy.

**When to use:** When the same Cloud Armor WAF policy must protect different services with different false-positive profiles. Superset/Metabase (BI project) trigger SQLi rules; Keycloak triggers session fixation rules; Django admin triggers method enforcement.

**Trade-offs:** Exclusions live in `sec/waf`, not in the service's own module. A developer adding a new microservice cannot self-service add WAF exclusions — they must modify `sec/waf`. This is intentional: WAF exclusions are a security decision, not a per-service concern.

**Example:**

```hcl
# sec/waf/locals.tf — rule set composition
locals {
  # Base rules — identical across all environments
  waf_rules_base = {
    "1000" = { ... ip whitelist ... }
    "1010" = { ... user-agent blocking ... }
    "1030" = { action = "deny(403)", preview = true, expr = "evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sqli-v33-stable')" }
    # ... other OWASP rules ...
    "1170" = { ... rate limiting ... }
  }

  # BI-specific: superset and metabase are SQL query builders.
  # SQLi rules will false-positive on valid SQL queries submitted by authenticated users.
  # Exclude SQLi inspection for known BI tool hosts.
  waf_rules_bi = merge(local.waf_rules_base, {
    "1030" = {
      action         = "deny(403)"
      description    = "SQLi - con exclusion para superset/metabase"
      preview        = true
      expr           = "evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sqli-v33-stable') && !request.headers['host'].matches('(?i:superset|metabase)')"
    }
  })

  # QA-specific: may need different IP whitelist
  waf_rules_qa = merge(local.waf_rules_base, {
    "1000" = {
      action         = "allow"
      description    = "IPs de confianza - QA"
      preview        = false
      versioned_expr = "SRC_IPS_V1"
      src_ip_ranges  = ["34.23.50.140"]  # QA NAT IP
    }
  })

  waf_rules_prod = merge(local.waf_rules_base, {
    "1000" = {
      action         = "allow"
      description    = "IPs de confianza - Prod"
      preview        = false
      versioned_expr = "SRC_IPS_V1"
      src_ip_ranges  = ["34.74.192.228"]  # Prod NAT IP
    }
  })
}
```

### Pattern 4: Workspace-Conditional Policy Reference in Consumer Modules

**What:** Consumer modules that run across multiple workspaces (qa/staging/prod) select the correct WAF policy self_link from remote state based on `terraform.workspace`.

**When to use:** `apps/gke`, `apps/frontends`, `apps/airflow`, `apps/apps` are all multi-workspace. They must reference the right policy for their project.

**Trade-offs:** Adds a conditional expression to the `cloud_armor_policy` parameter. Simple and consistent with existing workspace-based logic already present in these modules (e.g., `neg_ids[terraform.workspace]` pattern).

**Example:**

```hcl
# apps/gke/load-balancer.tf
locals {
  waf_policy_map = {
    qa      = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.qa_policy_self_link
    staging = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.staging_policy_self_link
    prod    = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.prod_policy_self_link
  }
}

module "gke-apps-load-balancer" {
  # ...
  cloud_armor_policy = local.waf_policy_map[terraform.workspace]
}
```

For single-workspace modules (`common/apps` runs in `sha`, `bi/apps` runs in `bi`), use the specific output directly:

```hcl
# common/apps/load-balancer.tf
cloud_armor_policy = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.sha_policy_self_link

# bi/apps/load-balancer.tf
cloud_armor_policy = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.bi_policy_self_link
```

## Data Flow

### WAF Policy Deployment Flow

```
1. Engineer modifies sec/waf/waf.tf or locals.tf
        ↓
2. terraform apply (workspace: sec)
   → deploys google_compute_security_policy to qa-apps-454414
   → deploys google_compute_security_policy to prod-apps-454414
   → deploys google_compute_security_policy to shared-016
   → deploys google_compute_security_policy to liftit-bi
   → writes outputs to GCS: liftit-tf-state/sec/waf/sec.tfstate
        ↓
3. Consumer module runs (e.g., apps/gke, workspace: qa)
   → reads data.terraform_remote_state.waf (workspace=sec)
   → gets outputs.qa_policy_self_link
   → passes to module.gke-apps-load-balancer cloud_armor_policy param
   → tf-modules//load-balancer sets security_policy on google_compute_backend_service
        ↓
4. GCP attaches the Cloud Armor policy to the backend service
   → Traffic through the LB is inspected (preview mode: logged but not blocked)
```

### Rule Exclusion Addition Flow

```
1. Endpoint analysis identifies false positive (e.g., Superset SQL editor)
        ↓
2. Add exclusion to sec/waf/locals.tf (waf_rules_bi or new expr in rule)
        ↓
3. terraform apply (workspace: sec)
   → updates google_compute_security_policy_rule in liftit-bi project
        ↓
4. bi/apps LB module already references bi_policy_self_link — no change needed
   (Policy is updated in-place; no re-apply of consumer modules required)
```

### IP Whitelist Update Flow

```
sec/waf/waf.tf local.ip_whitelist[workspace]
        ↓ (currently per-workspace)
Target: move to per-project keys in locals.tf
local.ip_whitelist = {
  qa      = ["34.23.50.140"]       # qa-apps-454414 NAT
  staging = ["35.196.126.133"]     # stg-apps-454414 NAT
  prod    = ["34.74.192.228"]      # prod-apps-454414 NAT
  sha     = ["35.185.50.62"]       # shared-016 NAT
  bi      = [...]                  # liftit-bi NAT (add when known)
  sec     = ["35.227.65.152"]      # security-454414 NAT
}
```

## New vs Modified Components

### NEW

| Component | What Changes | File |
|-----------|--------------|------|
| `sec/waf/providers.tf` | Add provider aliases for qa, prod, sha, bi | New file (or extend existing) |
| `sec/waf/waf.tf` | Replace single module call with one per project | Rewrite |
| `sec/waf/outputs.tf` | Export `{project}_policy_self_link` per project | Rewrite |
| `sec/waf/locals.tf` | Add `waf_rules_{env}` locals for per-env exclusions | Extend |

### MODIFIED

| Component | What Changes | File |
|-----------|--------------|------|
| `apps/gke/remote-state.tf` | Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source | Add block |
| `apps/gke/load-balancer.tf` | Set `cloud_armor_policy = waf_policy_map[workspace]` | Change 1 line |
| `apps/frontends/remote-state.tf` | Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source | Add block |
| `apps/frontends/load-balancer.tf` | Set `cloud_armor_policy = waf_policy_map[workspace]` | Change 1 line |
| `apps/airflow/remote-state.tf` | Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source | Add block |
| `apps/airflow/load-balancer.tf` | Set `cloud_armor_policy = waf_policy_map[workspace]` | Change 1 line |
| `apps/apps/remote-state.tf` | Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source | Add block |
| `apps/apps/load-balancer.tf` | Set `cloud_armor_policy = waf_policy_map[workspace]` | Change 1 line |
| `common/apps/remote-state.tf` | Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source | Add block |
| `common/apps/load-balancer.tf` | Set `cloud_armor_policy = sha_policy_self_link` | Change 1 line |
| `bi/apps/remote-state.tf` | Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source | Add block |
| `bi/apps/load-balancer.tf` | Set `cloud_armor_policy = bi_policy_self_link` | Change 1 line |
| `bi/wrenai-poc/remote-state.tf` | Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source | Add block |
| `bi/wrenai-poc/load-balancer.tf` | Set `cloud_armor_policy = bi_policy_self_link` | Change 1 line |

### UNCHANGED

| Component | Reason |
|-----------|--------|
| `tf-modules//waf` | Private module is already correct — takes `rules` map, creates policy + rules |
| `tf-modules//load-balancer` | Already accepts `cloud_armor_policy` string — no interface change needed |
| `sec/waf/backend.tf` | State stays at `liftit-tf-state/sec/waf`, workspace `sec` |
| `apps/gke/gke.tf` | GKE cluster unaffected |
| `sec/waf/remote-state.tf` | Folder + DNS remote state unchanged |

## Build Order

The following sequence must be respected due to remote state dependencies:

```
Step 1: sec/waf  (workspace: sec)
   → Deploys policies to qa-apps-454414, prod-apps-454414, shared-016, liftit-bi
   → Writes self_links to GCS state
   → MUST complete before any LB consumer module runs

Step 2 (parallel, QA milestone only):
   → apps/gke        (workspace: qa)   — reads qa_policy_self_link
   → apps/frontends  (workspace: qa)   — reads qa_policy_self_link
   → apps/airflow    (workspace: qa)   — reads qa_policy_self_link
   → apps/apps       (workspace: qa)   — reads qa_policy_self_link

   These can run in parallel since they only depend on sec/waf state output.

Step 3 (future — staging/prod rollout):
   → apps/gke        (workspace: staging/prod)
   → apps/frontends  (workspace: staging/prod)
   → etc.
```

## Integration Points

### IAM Requirements

The Terraform service account running `sec/waf` currently has permissions in `security-454414`. To deploy policies to other projects, it needs:

| Permission | Required For |
|------------|-------------|
| `compute.securityPolicies.create` | Creating policies in qa/prod/sha/bi projects |
| `compute.securityPolicies.update` | Updating rules |
| `compute.securityPolicies.delete` | Cleanup |
| `compute.securityPolicies.use` | Required for backend service attachment (granted to LB project SA) |

The Terraform SA in `sec` must be granted `roles/compute.securityAdmin` in each target project, OR the per-project Terraform SAs must be used via provider credential overrides.

**Recommended:** Grant `roles/compute.securityAdmin` to the `sec` workspace Terraform SA in each target project:
- `qa-apps-454414`
- `prod-apps-454414`
- `shared-016`
- `liftit-bi`

### WAF Module Interface Contract

The private `tf-modules//waf` module must output `policy_self_link` (or `policy_name`) for consumption by `sec/waf/outputs.tf`. Based on the current output in `sec/waf/outputs.tf`:

```hcl

}

output "prod_policy_name" {
```

Exclusions address false positives for high-risk services. Use CEL expressions in the rule `expr` field combined with host header matching, rather than `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusion blocks, because the existing `tf-modules//waf` rule schema uses `expr` strings. Adding `preconfigured_waf_config` blocks would require changes to the private module interface.

```hcl
# Rule 1030 — SQLi with Superset/Metabase exclusion (BI policy only)
"1030" = {
  action      = "deny(403)"
  description = "SQLi - excluye superset y metabase (BI)"
  preview     = true

}
```

```hcl
# Rule 1080 — Method enforcement with Django admin exclusion
"1080" = {
  action      = "deny(403)"
  description = "Method enforcement - excluye Django admin"
  preview     = true
  expr        = "evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('methodenforcement-v33-stable') && !request.path.startsWith('/admin/')"
```

1. **Critical architectural constraint:** Cloud Armor `google_compute_security_policy` is project-scoped. A policy in `security-454414` cannot be attached to backend services in `qa-apps-454414`, `prod-apps-454414`, `liftit-bi`, or `shared-016`. The original "single centralized policy in sec project" concept is architecturally invalid at the GCP API level.

2. **Correct centralization pattern:** Deploy identical policies into each target project from a single `sec/waf` Terraform state using multi-provider aliases (`provider "google" { alias = "qa"; project = "qa-apps-454414" }`). One `terraform apply` updates all projects atomically. This is the correct interpretation of "centralized" for Cloud Armor.

3. **Remote state propagation works as-is:** The existing `terraform_remote_state` pattern (already used for KMS, VPC, SSL) extends cleanly to WAF policy names. Consumer modules add one `data` block and change `cloud_armor_policy = null` to `= data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.{env}_policy_name`. 5. **IAM prerequisite:** The `sec` workspace Terraform SA must receive `roles/compute.securityAdmin` in `qa-apps-454414`, `prod-apps-454414`, `shared-016`, and `liftit-bi` — currently it likely only has this in `security-454414`.

# Pitfalls Research

**Domain:** Cloud Armor WAF activation on existing multi-project GCP infrastructure
**Researched:** 2026-02-24
**Confidence:** HIGH (official Google documentation) / MEDIUM (community patterns) / LOW (inferred from infrastructure analysis)

---

## Critical Pitfalls

### Pitfall 1: Cross-Project Policy Attachment Is Not Straightforward

**What goes wrong:**
The planned architecture centralize the WAF policy in the `sec` project (security-454414) and reference it from load balancers in `qa`, `prod`, `bi`, and `sha` projects. Cloud Armor security policies are project-scoped resources. A `google_compute_backend_service` in project `qa-apps-454414` cannot attach a `google_compute_security_policy` that lives in `security-454414` using a simple name reference. Only self_links work — and even self_links require the backend service's project to have authorization to use the foreign policy. Cross-project service referencing for Cloud Armor explicitly requires Cloud Armor Enterprise enrollment for both projects under the same billing account.

**Why it happens:**
The architecture decision to centralize the policy in `sec` follows the same pattern used for KMS (centralized in `sec`), but KMS cross-project reference is a first-class GCP feature. Cloud Armor cross-project policy reference is not — it is an Enterprise tier feature. The existing `sec/waf/outputs.tf` only exports `waf_policy_name` (a string name), not the `self_link`. Even if the self_link were exported via remote state, attaching it to a backend service in a different project would fail without Enterprise enrollment.

**How to avoid:**
Two viable options exist:

Option A — Per-project policies (no Enterprise required): Keep the existing pattern of one policy per workspace. The `sec/waf` module already creates `liftit-waf-${workspace}`. Each workspace's load balancer references its own local policy. Use Terraform module composition to keep rules DRY. This is the current architecture and requires zero cross-project IAM changes.

Option B — Hierarchical policy (Enterprise auto-enrolled): Use `google_compute_organization_security_policy` instead of `google_compute_security_policy`. Hierarchical policies attach at org/folder level and automatically cover all projects below. This triggers automatic Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo enrollment — verify cost implications before choosing this path.

Do NOT assume a policy self_link from the `sec` project can be passed to a `google_compute_backend_service` in the `qa` project without Enterprise.

**Warning signs:**
- Terraform plan shows `google_compute_backend_service.security_policy` accepting a self_link from a different project
- No Cloud Armor Enterprise subscription visible in billing
- Apply succeeds but security policy is not actually enforced (no logs appear)

**Phase to address:**
Phase 1 (Architecture Decision). This must be resolved before any Terraform code is written. Validate the cross-project approach with a minimal test: create a policy in `sec`, attempt to attach it to a backend service in `qa` via self_link, and observe whether it applies.

---

### Pitfall 2: Method Enforcement Rule Blocks All REST API Traffic

**What goes wrong:**
Rule `1080` uses `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('methodenforcement-v33-stable')`. The OWASP CRS method enforcement ruleset (rule owasp-crs-v030301-id911100) defines an allowed methods list. By default, only GET, HEAD, POST, and OPTIONS pass. PUT, DELETE, and PATCH are blocked. Every microservice in the GKE cluster uses standard REST conventions with PUT, DELETE, and PATCH. When this rule is activated (preview=false), all update/delete REST operations across all 35+ microservices will return 403.

**Why it happens:**
The OWASP CRS method enforcement rule was designed for traditional web applications that only use GET and POST. Modern REST APIs universally use PUT/PATCH/DELETE. Cloud Armor does not expose the CRS configuration option to extend the allowed methods list — unlike self-hosted ModSecurity. The only workaround is path-based exclusions or disabling the rule entirely.

**How to avoid:**
Either disable the method enforcement rule entirely (recommended for a REST microservices architecture), or create explicit allow rules before rule `1080` for each HTTP method used. Given the API-centric nature of all Liftit services, the method enforcement rule provides near-zero value and maximum false positive risk. The correct decision is to exclude PUT, DELETE, and PATCH globally or drop this rule from the active set.

Log analysis during preview mode will show volume: expect 100% of PUT/PATCH/DELETE requests to appear as would-be violations.

**Warning signs:**
- During preview mode analysis, rule 1080 appears in every API update/delete operation log entry
- Any endpoint with standard CRUD patterns shows violations against this rule

**Phase to address:**
Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis). When analyzing preview logs, rule 1080 will be the most frequently triggered rule by volume. Flag it immediately for exclusion or removal before activation.

---

### Pitfall 3: Superset and Metabase Will Be Completely Broken by SQLi Rules

**What goes wrong:**
Superset and Metabase are SQL query builder tools. Their core function is to transmit raw SQL queries from the browser to the backend via HTTP POST/PUT request bodies. The SQLi rule (`1030`, `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sqli-v33-stable')`) will detect these legitimate SQL payloads as SQL injection attacks and block them. Every chart creation, dashboard query, and dataset exploration operation will return 403.

The `json-sqli-canary` rule (`1160`) compounds this: Superset's API uses JSON request bodies containing SQL queries, meaning every API call that includes a SQL query in JSON format triggers this rule too.

**Why it happens:**
WAF SQLi detection operates on pattern matching, not context. A `SELECT orders.id, customers.name FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id` payload is indistinguishable from SQL injection to a pattern-matching WAF. Metabase's `/api/card` endpoint (PUT and POST) and Superset's `/api/v1/chart/` and `/api/v1/dataset/` endpoints all send raw SQL in request bodies.

**How to avoid:**
Add request path exclusions for Superset and Metabase backend endpoints from the SQLi rules before activation. Both tools use prepared statements internally, making external SQLi rules redundant for their traffic.

Terraform exclusion pattern:
```hcl
preconfigured_waf_config {
  exclusion {
    target_rule_set = "sqli-v33-stable"
    request_uri {
      op    = "STARTS_WITH"
      value = "/api/"
    }
  }
}
```

The bi-apps LB hosts both Metabase and Superset. The Superset UI also allows custom SQL, meaning the exclusion needs to cover the entire `/api/` path tree for both applications.

**Warning signs:**
- Rule 1030 and 1160 appear in preview logs for ALL Superset and Metabase traffic that involves chart creation or SQL editing

**Phase to address:**
Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis). Superset and Metabase endpoints must be catalogued and excluded from SQLi rules before activation. This is a guaranteed false positive, not a maybe.

---

### Pitfall 4: Keycloak Auth Flows Trigger Multiple WAF Rules Simultaneously

**What goes wrong:**
Keycloak generates complex authentication flows involving:
- Long JWT access tokens in Authorization headers (may trigger XSS or RCE pattern detection)
- Base64-encoded session data in cookies (may trigger sessionfixation rules)
- PKCE code_challenge parameters with high-entropy strings (may trigger scanner detection)
- Special characters in password fields (`!@#$%^&*`) that trigger SQLi or XSS patterns
- SAML assertion payloads in POST bodies that contain XML with encoded characters

Users attempting login with complex passwords or using SAML-based SSO may receive 403 responses. Since Keycloak is the authentication gateway for the entire platform, blocking it effectively locks out all users.

**Why it happens:**
The Keycloak community has documented (GitHub Discussion #35586) that there is "no perfect solution" for WAF compatibility — every deployment requires custom exclusion tuning. The Keycloak login flow sends credentials in POST body fields that WAF rules interpret as potential attacks. Session fixation rules are particularly problematic because Keycloak deliberately manages session tokens across redirects (which is what session fixation protection is designed to prevent, but Keycloak's implementation is legitimate).

**How to avoid:**
Apply path-based exclusions to all Keycloak endpoints before activation:
- `/auth/realms/*/protocol/openid-connect/token` (token endpoint)
- `/auth/realms/*/protocol/openid-connect/auth` (authorization endpoint)
- `/auth/admin/*` (admin console)
- `/auth/realms/*/login-actions/*` (login flows)

Test specifically with: password login using special characters, SAML SSO flows, token refresh operations, and admin console access.

**Warning signs:**
- Any preview log entry for `keycloak.*` hostnames showing violations against sessionfixation, xss, or sqli rules
- Rule 1120 (sessionfixation) appearing frequently for `/auth/` paths

**Phase to address:**
Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis) with dedicated Keycloak test scenario. Phase 3 (Fine-tuning) for exclusion configuration.

---

### Pitfall 5: Logging Is Not Enabled by Default — Silent Failures

**What goes wrong:**
Cloud Armor request logging is disabled by default for all backend services. The WAF can be attached to a load balancer in preview mode and appear to be working — the Terraform apply succeeds, the policy is associated — but zero logs are generated. There is no visibility into what the WAF is evaluating, no evidence of what would be blocked, and no ability to detect false positives. The entire preview phase analysis produces nothing.

**Why it happens:**
GCP disables backend service logging by default to avoid billing surprises. Engineers attaching the WAF policy assume logging is part of the policy, not the backend service. The `google_compute_backend_service` resource has a separate `log_config` block that defaults to disabled. This is separate from Cloud Armor verbose logging.

**How to avoid:**
Explicitly enable logging on every backend service that has the WAF policy attached. In the load-balancer module, ensure `log_config { enable = true, sample_rate = 1.0 }` is set during the analysis phase. Reduce sample_rate to 0.1 after tuning is complete if log volume is a concern.

The critical log filter for false positive detection:
```
resource.type="http_load_balancer"
jsonPayload.enforcedSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"
```

For preview mode violations (would-have-been-blocked):
```
resource.type="http_load_balancer"
jsonPayload.previewSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"
```

**Warning signs:**
- No Cloud Armor log entries in Cloud Logging after policy attachment
- The `log_config` block is absent from the backend service Terraform resource

**Phase to address:**
Phase 1 (Policy Attachment). Enable logging as part of the same Terraform apply that attaches the WAF policy. Never attach a WAF policy without logging enabled.

---

### Pitfall 6: Rate Limiting Rule Blocks Cloud Scheduler Jobs

**What goes wrong:**
Rule `1170` bans IPs exceeding 1000 req/min (with a ban threshold of 2000 req/min for 5 minutes). Cloud Scheduler jobs call microservice endpoints on scheduled intervals. Multiple scheduler jobs calling the same service in a burst — or a single high-frequency job like `reenviar-ordenes-pendientes-pricesmart` (every 5 minutes), `resync_services_lms_to_tms` (every 15 minutes), or `advances-payment-request-confirm` (every 15 minutes) — originate from Google Cloud infrastructure IPs that are shared and not predictable in advance. A scheduled batch spike can trigger the rate ban, causing a 5-minute service blackout for all traffic from the affected IP range.

**Why it happens:**
Cloud Scheduler requests originate from Google's shared infrastructure, not from dedicated static IPs. The source IP of a scheduler job cannot be whitelisted because it is not fixed. During integration tests or batch runs, multiple scheduler jobs executing in parallel from the same underlying Google infrastructure IP can collectively exceed the 1000 req/min threshold, triggering the ban.

The existing IP whitelist (rule 1000) only includes the NAT gateway IPs for each workspace — not the scheduler's originating IPs.

**How to avoid:**
Keep rule 1170 (rate limit) in preview mode longer than other rules. Independently analyze rate-limit preview log entries to understand whether Google Scheduler source IPs appear in violation logs. Consider using `THROTTLE` action instead of `rate_based_ban` — throttle limits the rate without banning the source, which prevents legitimate services from being locked out entirely.

Alternatively, add a CIDR allowlist for Google's health check and scheduler IP ranges (documented by Google) with higher priority than rule 1170.

**Warning signs:**
- Preview logs showing rule 1170 triggered by `googleapis.com` user-agents or scheduler service accounts
- 403 responses appearing for scheduled jobs in Cloud Scheduler execution history

**Phase to address:**
Phase 3 (Fine-tuning). Rate limit rule analysis requires traffic pattern data from preview logs. Validate separately from OWASP rules.

---

### Pitfall 7: File Upload Endpoints Bypassed By the 8KB Body Inspection Limit

**What goes wrong:**
Cloud Armor only inspects the first 8,192 bytes of HTTP POST/PUT request bodies. Excel-loader, lms-excel-loader, and docscan-service handle large file uploads (Excel files, scanned documents) that are far larger than 8KB. Cloud Armor scans only the first 8KB and then passes the rest through unchecked — meaning a malicious payload embedded after the 8KB mark in a multi-part upload bypasses all WAF inspection. This creates a security gap that is invisible unless explicitly addressed.

**Why it happens:**
This is a documented GCP WAF architecture limitation, not a configuration error. The design assumption is that WAF inspection applies to request metadata and small payloads, not large binary file uploads. The documentation notes this default pass-through behavior explicitly.

**How to avoid:**
Add a custom Cloud Armor rule that blocks requests where `Content-Length > 8192` unless the request is to an explicitly allowed upload endpoint. For the known upload endpoints (excel-loader, lms-excel-loader, docscan-service), add path-specific rules that allow large payloads but flag them for application-level validation.

Example rule (to be added to waf.tf):
```hcl
"900" = {
  action      = "deny(403)"
  description = "Block oversized requests except on upload endpoints"
  preview     = true
  expr        = "int(request.headers['content-length']) > 8192 && !request.path.matches('/upload/.*') && !request.path.matches('/api/upload.*')"
}
```

This pitfall is not about false positives — it is about a security gap that the WAF appears to close but does not.

**Warning signs:**
- No custom Content-Length rule in the policy
- File upload endpoints not explicitly listed in WAF exclusion documentation

**Phase to address:**
Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis). Document all file upload endpoints and their expected payload sizes. Phase 3 (Fine-tuning) to add the Content-Length protection rule.

---

### Pitfall 8: Activating Rules Individually Without Incremental Traffic Analysis

**What goes wrong:**
All 17 OWASP rules are currently in preview mode. The naive activation path is to flip all `preview = false` in one apply. This creates an immediately undebuggable situation: when users start getting 403 errors, there is no way to determine which of the 17 rules is responsible without examining individual log entries. Even with logs enabled, multiple rules may fire simultaneously on the same request, complicating root cause analysis.

**Why it happens:**
It is tempting to treat preview-to-active as a single toggle since all the rules exist. The assumption is "we checked the logs, it looks fine." But preview log analysis at low traffic volume may miss edge cases that appear at production load or with specific user workflows.

**How to avoid:**
Activate rules one at a time or in logical groups, with a 24-48 hour monitoring window between each activation. Suggested activation order (least risky to most risky for this infrastructure):

1. Scanner detection (1090) — lowest false positive rate for API services
2. LFI (1050), RFI (1070) — rarely triggered by legitimate REST traffic
3. RCE (1060) — low risk for standard application payloads
4. Java (1130), NodeJS (1140) — relevant to tech stack but focused signatures
5. Protocol attacks (1100) — low false positive for standard HTTP/HTTPS
6. XSS (1040) — moderate risk; inspect carefully for admin panel traffic
7. Session fixation (1120) — activate only after Keycloak exclusions are confirmed
8. SQLi (1030), JSON-SQLi (1160) — activate only after BI tool exclusions confirmed
9. Method enforcement (1080) — requires careful review; likely disable for REST APIs
10. Rate limiting (1170) — activate last; validate scheduler traffic first

**Warning signs:**
- Terraform plan shows all rules switching to `preview = false` in one change
- No documented per-rule activation schedule in the milestone plan

**Phase to address:**
Phase 4 (Activation). The phase must explicitly define an incremental activation sequence, not a bulk toggle.

---

## Technical Debt Patterns

| Shortcut | Immediate Benefit | Long-term Cost | When Acceptable |
|----------|-------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| Activate all rules simultaneously | Faster to production-active state | Undebuggable false positives; impossible to isolate which rule caused which error | Never |
| Skip logging enablement | Lower Cloud Logging costs | No visibility into WAF behavior; blind WAF deployment | Never |
| Keep method enforcement rule active | Appears more "complete" coverage | Blocks all PUT/DELETE/PATCH REST traffic; major outage | Never for REST API infrastructure |
| Same policy for BI tools and microservices | Simpler Terraform | SQLi rules must be disabled globally because of Superset/Metabase, weakening protection for other services | Only if separate LBs/policies are not feasible |
| Skip cross-project architecture validation | Faster initial implementation | Discover Enterprise tier requirement mid-milestone; forced architecture change under time pressure | Never |
| Use `cve-canary` without version pinning | Always current CVE coverage | Rule set can change without notice, introducing new false positives unexpectedly | Never in production without a review gate |

---

## Integration Gotchas

| Integration | Common Mistake | Correct Approach |
|-------------|----------------|------------------|
| Keycloak | Applying WAF rules to all `/auth/` paths without exclusions | Add per-path exclusions for token endpoint, login-actions, and admin console before activation |
| Kong API Gateway | Assuming WAF inspection happens at the Kong layer | WAF operates at the LB layer before Kong; all requests through `gateway-*.liftit-sandbox.com` are inspected at the L7 LB, not at Kong itself |
| Superset / Metabase | Applying SQLi rules without path exclusions | Exclude `/api/` paths on the bi-apps LB from sqli and json-sqli rules before activation |
| Cloud Scheduler | Not accounting for scheduler source IPs in rate limit allowlist | Analyze scheduler source IPs from preview logs; consider THROTTLE instead of rate_based_ban |
| Django admin (support-administration, backoffice-api) | Django CSRF tokens in POST bodies triggering XSS or session fixation rules | Add path exclusions for `/admin/` and login endpoints; verify Django's csrftoken cookie does not trigger sessionfixation rules |
| Excel/document file uploads | Assuming WAF inspects entire file content | Cloud Armor only inspects first 8KB; add Content-Length protection rules for upload endpoints |
| Cloud Run services | `domain-map.tf` has `cloud_armor_policy = null` — Cloud Run domain mappings do not use the same backend service mechanism | Cloud Run domain mappings managed by `apps/cloudrun` use `google_cloud_run_domain_mapping`, not an LB backend service; Cloud Armor cannot be attached directly to Cloud Run domain mappings in this manner |

---

## Performance Traps

| Trap | Symptoms | Prevention | When It Breaks |
|------|----------|------------|----------------|
| Rate limiting set too low for batch operations | Scheduler jobs return 403 during batch runs; services intermittently unavailable | Monitor rate limit preview logs for 48 hours including batch windows before activation | Immediately upon activation if 30+ scheduler jobs run concurrently |
| Verbose logging enabled in production long-term | Cloud Logging costs spike; PII (tokens, passwords) appears in logs | Enable verbose logging only during tuning; disable after exclusions are confirmed | Continuously; costs accumulate daily |
| Full log sampling (sample_rate=1.0) kept post-tuning | High Cloud Logging ingestion costs for high-traffic services | Reduce to 0.1 after tuning is complete | At scale; 35+ microservices with full logging is expensive |
| Single security policy for all 7 LBs | BI tool exclusions (SQLi disabled) applied globally, weakening protection for core microservices | Use separate policy or per-backend exclusions; the bi-apps LB needs different tuning than gke-apps LB | Not a performance trap but a security degradation that is invisible |

---

## Security Mistakes

| Mistake | Risk | Prevention |
|---------|------|------------|
| Activating WAF without endpoint-specific exclusions for Superset/Metabase | 100% of SQL query builder operations blocked | Catalogue and exclude BI tool API endpoints from SQLi rules before activation |
| Relying solely on WAF for file upload security | Malicious payloads embedded after 8KB bypass all WAF inspection | Add Content-Length rule; implement application-level validation in upload services |
| Treating preview mode as "safe to ignore" | Preview logs contain the only evidence of what will break before activation; ignoring them means blind activation | Analyze every preview log entry; build a false positive register before any rule goes active |
| Not outputting policy `self_link` from `sec/waf` | Cannot reference policy from other modules even if cross-project is validated | Add `waf_policy_self_link` output to `sec/waf/outputs.tf` regardless of architecture choice |
| User-agent blocking (rule 1010) blocking monitoring tools | GoogleStackdriverMonitoring appears in the user-agent deny list (rule 1020 denies it) — the description says "Permitir" but the action is "deny(403)" | Rule 1020 as written BLOCKS uptime checks, not allows them. This is a configuration bug: the description and action contradict each other. Fix rule 1020 action to "allow" before activating |

---

## "Looks Done But Isn't" Checklist

- [ ] **Logging enabled**: `log_config { enable = true }` is set on every backend service — not just the policy attached. Verify in GCP Console that log entries appear after policy attachment.
- [ ] **Rule 1020 corrected**: The Stackdriver monitoring rule has `action = "deny(403)"` with a description that says "Permitir" (allow). This is a bug. Verify the intended behavior and fix before activating.
- [ ] **Cross-project attachment validated**: Confirm whether the centralized `sec` policy can attach to backends in `qa` project — do not assume; test with a real apply to a single non-critical backend service.
- [ ] **Method enforcement reviewed**: Confirm all HTTP methods used by GKE microservices are accounted for. PUT, DELETE, PATCH will be blocked by rule 1080.
- [ ] **BI tool exclusions documented**: Superset and Metabase SQLi exclusions are specified per endpoint path in Terraform before rule 1030 goes active.
- [ ] **Keycloak test coverage**: Authentication flows with special-character passwords, SAML SSO, and token refresh have all been tested in preview logs before activation.
- [ ] **Rate limit threshold validated**: 1000 req/min per IP has been verified against actual peak traffic metrics for the highest-volume services (tms-api, tracking-service, kong).
- [ ] **Cloud Run WAF gap acknowledged**: `apps/cloudrun` domain mappings cannot attach Cloud Armor; these services remain unprotected at the WAF layer regardless of this milestone.
- [ ] **8KB Content-Length rule added**: A custom rule blocking oversized requests to non-upload endpoints is added to the policy.
- [ ] **Activation sequence documented**: Each rule's activation is scheduled individually, not as a bulk toggle.

---

## Recovery Strategies

| Pitfall | Recovery Cost | Recovery Steps |
|---------|---------------|----------------|
| Wrong rule blocks production traffic after activation | HIGH | Set `preview = true` for the offending rule in Terraform; apply immediately; Terraform apply propagates in ~2 minutes; analyze logs to identify excluded paths |
| Rate ban locks out legitimate IPs | MEDIUM | Add the banned IP/range to the IP whitelist (rule 1000) with priority lower than 1000 but higher than 1170; ban expires in 300 seconds automatically |
| Cross-project attachment fails at apply time | MEDIUM | Fall back to per-project policy pattern; `sec/waf` already creates per-workspace policies; re-enable them in the target workspace |
| Superset/Metabase completely down after SQLi activation | HIGH | Immediately set rule 1030 and 1160 back to `preview = true`; add path exclusions for `/api/` on the bi-apps LB; re-activate with exclusions |
| Logging not enabled — no data for analysis | LOW | Enable `log_config` on backend service; wait 30-60 minutes for data to appear; preview analysis must restart from baseline |
| Rule 1020 blocks Stackdriver uptime checks | MEDIUM | Fix action from `deny(403)` to `allow` in waf.tf; apply; uptime checks resume immediately |

---

## Pitfall-to-Phase Mapping

| Pitfall | Prevention Phase | Verification |
|---------|------------------|--------------|
| Cross-project policy attachment | Phase 1: Architecture validation | Test apply of policy self_link to one QA backend service; check if enforcement appears in logs |
| Method enforcement breaks REST APIs | Phase 2: Endpoint analysis | Review preview logs for rule 1080; count PUT/DELETE/PATCH violation volume |
| Superset/Metabase SQLi false positives | Phase 2: BI tool endpoint catalogue | Zero rule 1030/1160 violations for normal BI workflows in preview logs |
| Keycloak auth flow false positives | Phase 2: Auth flow testing | Full Keycloak login test suite produces zero violations in preview logs |
| Logging not enabled | Phase 1: Policy attachment | Cloud Logging shows entries within 5 minutes of policy attach |
| Rate limiting blocks schedulers | Phase 2/3: Rate limit analysis | No rule 1170 violations from Google Cloud Scheduler source IPs in 48-hour preview window |
| 8KB file upload bypass | Phase 3: Fine-tuning | Content-Length rule added and tested with test upload exceeding 8KB |
| Bulk rule activation | Phase 4: Incremental activation | Each rule activated individually; 24-hour monitoring window documented between activations |
| Rule 1020 config bug | Phase 1: Policy audit | Rule 1020 action verified correct before any LB attachment |

---

## Phase-Specific Warnings

| Phase Topic | Likely Pitfall | Mitigation |
|-------------|---------------|------------|
| Centralizing policy in sec project | Cross-project attachment requires Enterprise or architecture change | Validate attachment feasibility before committing to architecture |
| Attaching to bi-apps LB (Superset/Metabase) | SQLi rules will block all chart/query operations | Pre-define path exclusions in waf.tf before setting preview=false for rules 1030/1160 |
| Attaching to gke-apps LB (35+ microservices) | Method enforcement will block REST operations; rate limit may fire during batch | Keep rules 1080 and 1170 in preview longest; analyze per-service violation volume |
| Activating sessionfixation rule (1120) | Keycloak uses cross-redirect session management that looks like fixation | Require Keycloak endpoint exclusions to be merged before this rule goes active |
| Activating on keycloak backend | Auth outage blocks all users | Test separately with health-check validation; have rollback committed before applying |
| Activating on Kong gateway backend | Kong proxies to all downstream services; a false positive here blocks everything routed through Kong | Activate on Kong last; it must be the final service to get active WAF enforcement |

---

## RESEARCH COMPLETE

**Project:** Cloud Armor WAF Implementation — Liftit GCP Infrastructure
**Mode:** Pitfalls Research (adding WAF to existing production system)
**Confidence:** HIGH (critical findings backed by official documentation and direct code inspection)

### Key Findings

- **Architecture-blocking issue discovered**: Cross-project Cloud Armor policy attachment (sec project -> qa/prod/bi backends) requires Cloud Armor Enterprise enrollment. The centralized policy architecture as planned cannot work without either Enterprise tier or architecture rethink to per-project policies.

- **Active configuration bug found**: Rule 1020 in `sec/waf/waf.tf` has `action = "deny(403)"` with description "Permitir GoogleStackdriverMonitoring-UptimeChecks" — it will block uptime checks, not allow them. Must be fixed before any LB attachment.

- **Three guaranteed false positives identified**: (1) Method enforcement rule (1080) blocks PUT/DELETE/PATCH across all 35+ microservices; (2) SQLi rules (1030/1160) block 100% of Superset and Metabase operations; (3) Rate limiting (1170) may block Cloud Scheduler jobs from Google shared infrastructure IPs.

- **Logging is disabled by default**: WAF policy can be attached silently with zero log output. Must explicitly enable `log_config` on backend services to have any visibility during preview analysis.

- **8KB inspection gap**: File upload endpoints (excel-loader, lms-excel-loader, docscan-service) are only partially inspected — malicious payloads embedded after 8KB bypass the WAF entirely.

### Files Created

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/home/jhonortiz/devops/tf-infrastructure/.planning/research/PITFALLS.md` | Domain pitfalls with 8 critical issues, integration gotchas, recovery strategies, and phase mapping |

### Confidence Assessment

| Area | Level | Reason |
|------|-------|--------|
| Cross-project architecture limitation | HIGH | Official GCP documentation explicitly states Enterprise requirement for cross-project service referencing |
| Method enforcement false positives | HIGH | Official CRS documentation confirms only GET/HEAD/POST/OPTIONS allowed; community forum confirms workarounds needed |
| Superset/Metabase SQLi false positives | HIGH | Metabase community documentation + Cloud Armor docs confirm SQL payloads trigger WAF |
| Logging disabled by default | HIGH | Official request logging documentation explicitly states disabled by default |
| Rate limiting and schedulers | MEDIUM | Behavior inferred from rate limiting docs + scheduler IP non-determinism |
| Keycloak false positives | MEDIUM | Community evidence exists; specific rule exclusions require empirical testing |
| 8KB bypass | HIGH | Official GCP WAF documentation + security research publication |
| Rule 1020 configuration bug | HIGH | Direct code inspection of existing waf.tf |

### Roadmap Implications

1. **Phase 1 must include architecture validation** for cross-project attachment before any other work — this could require a complete architecture change (Enterprise tier vs. per-project policies).
2. **Fix rule 1020 before any LB attachment** — it is a configuration bug that blocks Google's own monitoring.
3. **Endpoint analysis phase must be explicit** about Superset/Metabase and Keycloak as highest-risk services with guaranteed false positives.
4. **Incremental rule activation is mandatory** — activating all 17 rules at once creates an undebuggable situation.
5. **BI tools need a separate exclusion strategy** from core microservices — consider whether they warrant a separate WAF policy or per-backend exclusion configs.

### Open Questions

- Does Liftit have Cloud Armor Enterprise? Verify in GCP Console before proceeding with centralized policy architecture.
- What are the actual HTTP methods used by each microservice? (PUT/DELETE/PATCH volume is unknown without log analysis)
- What is the peak request rate for tms-api and kong during batch operations? (Rate limit threshold validation)
- Do any microservices use PHP, Java, or Node.js runtime-specific patterns that would trigger the php/java/nodejs rules at sensitivity level 1?

1→# Stack Research
     2→
     3→**Domain:** Google Cloud Armor WAF — Terraform/GCP production deployment
     4→**Researched:** 2026-02-24
     5→**Confidence:** HIGH (GCP official docs + direct codebase inspection)
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Recommended Stack
    10→
    11→### Core Technologies
    12→
    13→| Technology | Version | Purpose | Why Recommended |
    14→|------------|---------|---------|-----------------|
    15→| Terraform | `~> 1.14` | IaC orchestration | Already in use across all 35 modules; no change needed |
    16→| Google Provider | `~> 7.0` | GCP resource management | Already in use; includes full support for `google_compute_security_policy_rule` with `preconfigured_waf_config` |
    17→| `google_compute_security_policy` | Google Provider ~> 7.0 | WAF policy container | Native GCP resource; already used via `tf-modules//waf` |
    18→| `google_compute_security_policy_rule` | Google Provider ~> 7.0 | Individual WAF rules | Supports `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusion blocks needed for tuning |
    19→| `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf()` | Current (replaces deprecated `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr`) | Expression to invoke OWASP rule sets | The only function that inspects both request headers AND body; required for effective WAF |
    20→
    21→### Preconfigured Rule Set Versions
    22→
    23→| Rule Set | Use Version | Notes |
    24→|----------|-------------|-------|
    25→| `sqli-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable; current for this milestone |
    26→| `xss-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    27→| `lfi-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    28→| `rce-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    29→| `rfi-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    30→| `methodenforcement-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    31→| `scannerdetection-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    32→| `protocolattack-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    33→| `php-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    34→| `sessionfixation-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    35→| `java-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    36→| `nodejs-v33-stable` | Keep as-is | CRS 3.3 stable |
    37→| `cve-canary` | Keep as-is | No stable version; canary is the only option for CVE rules; updated December 2025 with CVE-2025-55182 signatures |
    38→| `json-sqli-canary` | Keep as-is | No stable version; canary is the only option |
    39→
    40→**v33-stable is current.** There is no v40 or higher. Google's next version after CRS 3.3 has not been released as of February 2026. Upgrading to v33-canary is out of scope for this milestone (per PROJECT.md).
    41→
    42→**CRS 3.0 (`sqli-stable`, etc.) is legacy.** Excluded from consideration — v33 provides broader coverage including Java and NodeJS attack types absent from v30.
    43→
    44→### Terraform Resources Required
    45→
    46→| Resource | Purpose | Gap vs Current |
    47→|----------|---------|----------------|
    48→| `google_compute_security_policy` | WAF policy container | Already in `tf-modules//waf`; no change |
    49→| `google_compute_security_policy_rule` | Per-rule configuration | Already in `tf-modules//waf`; needs `preconfigured_waf_config` block for exclusions |
    50→| `google_compute_backend_service.security_policy` | Attaches policy to LB backend | Currently `null`; needs policy self_link or name |
    51→| `terraform_remote_state` | Cross-workspace data source | Pattern already used; needed to read `waf_policy_name` from sec workspace |
    52→
    53→### Rule Tuning: `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf` Syntax
    54→
    55→The existing rules use the deprecated `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr`. All new and modified rules should use `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf`:
    56→
    57→```hcl
    58→# DEPRECATED (current usage in waf.tf):
    59→expr = "evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sqli-v33-stable')"
    60→
    61→# CURRENT (recommended):
    62→expr = "evaluatePreconfiguredWaf('sqli-v33-stable', {'sensitivity': 1})"
    63→
    64→# With opt-out for specific signatures (false positive tuning):
    65→expr = "evaluatePreconfiguredWaf('sqli-v33-stable', {'sensitivity': 1, 'opt_out_rule_ids': ['owasp-crs-id942440-sqli', 'owasp-crs-id942450-sqli']})"
    66→
    67→# With opt-in only (sensitivity 0 = disable all except named):
    68→expr = "evaluatePreconfiguredWaf('json-sqli-canary', {'sensitivity': 0, 'opt_in_rule_ids': ['owasp-crs-id942550-sqli']})"
    69→```
    70→
    71→**Sensitivity levels (1–4):** Lower = fewer false positives, higher confidence. Higher = more aggressive, more false positives. Start at `sensitivity: 1` for high-risk services (Keycloak, Superset, Metabase, Backoffice API).
    72→
    73→### Exclusion Block Syntax (for `google_compute_security_policy_rule`)
    74→
    75→For per-service exclusions, the `preconfigured_waf_config` block in `google_compute_security_policy_rule`:
    76→
    77→```hcl
    78→resource "google_compute_security_policy_rule" "sqli_rule" {
    79→  security_policy = google_compute_security_policy.cloud_armor_policy.name
    80→  priority        = 1030
    81→  action          = "deny(403)"
    82→  preview         = true
    83→  description     = "SQLi - sqli-v33-stable"
    84→
    85→  match {
    86→    expr {
    87→      expression = "evaluatePreconfiguredWaf('sqli-v33-stable', {'sensitivity': 1})"
    88→    }
    89→  }
    90→
    91→  preconfigured_waf_config {
    92→    exclusion {
    93→      target_rule_set = "sqli-v33-stable"
    94→      # Omit target_rule_ids to exclude all rules in this set for matched requests
    95→      # OR specify individual rule IDs:
    96→      target_rule_ids = ["owasp-crs-id942440-sqli"]
    97→
    98→      request_header {
    99→        operator = "STARTS_WITH"
   100→        value    = "Authorization: Bearer"
   101→      }
   102→      request_cookie {
   103→        operator = "EQUALS_ANY"
   104→        # No value needed when operator is EQUALS_ANY
   105→      }
   106→    }
   107→  }
   108→}
   109→```
   110→
   111→**IMPORTANT:** `preconfigured_waf_config` is on `google_compute_security_policy_rule`, NOT on `google_compute_security_policy`. The current `tf-modules//waf` module only uses the `google_compute_security_policy_rule` resource but does NOT expose a `preconfigured_waf_config` variable. This means the tf-modules//waf module needs extension or the exclusion rules must be added as separate `google_compute_security_policy_rule` resources in `sec/waf/waf.tf` directly.
   112→
   113→---
   114→
   115→## Cross-Project Policy Architecture: Critical Constraint
   116→
   117→### The Constraint
   118→
   119→Cloud Armor project-level security policies (the standard `google_compute_security_policy`) **cannot be directly referenced cross-project** without Cloud Armor Enterprise enrollment. Specifically:
   120→
   121→> "If you use cross-project service referencing, both the frontend and backend service projects must be enrolled in Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual."
   122→
   123→This **blocks the original architecture goal** of centralizing one policy in `sec` and referencing it from `qa`, `bi`, `prod`, etc. as a simple self_link.
   124→
   125→### Available Approaches
   126→
   127→**Option A: One Policy Per Workspace (current pattern — recommended for this milestone)**
   128→- Keep the existing pattern: sec/waf deploys a policy per workspace (qa, staging, prod, sha, sec)
   129→- Each LB module reads its own policy from sec/waf remote state via workspace
   130→- Policy name follows `liftit-waf-${terraform.workspace}`
   131→- The `cloud_armor_policy` parameter already accepts a policy name string (not self_link)
   132→- Attach pattern: `cloud_armor_policy = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.waf_policy_name`
   133→
   134→This is the zero-cost approach. All 7 LB modules already accept `cloud_armor_policy`. No cross-project IAM needed. Policies diverge per environment which is actually desirable (QA can be looser than prod).
   135→
   136→**Option B: Hierarchical Security Policies (org/folder level)**
   137→- Requires Cloud Armor Enterprise enrollment ($200/month/project minimum, or $3,000/month Annual)
   138→- Created at org or folder level, not within a project
   139→- Applied to all projects under the hierarchy node
   140→- Managed via `gcloud compute org-security-policies` — Terraform support is limited
   141→- **Not recommended** for this milestone: cost overhead, limited Terraform support, out of scope
   142→
   143→**Option C: Terraform-managed policy replication via shared locals**
   144→- Define rules in a shared Terraform locals/module, deploy identical policy per workspace
   145→- Works today without any Cloud Armor Enterprise
   146→- The `tf-modules//waf` pattern already does this — sec/waf deploys per workspace
   147→
   148→### Recommended Cross-Project Pattern (Remote State)
   149→
   150→Reading the policy name in other workspace modules:
   151→
   152→```hcl
   153→# In apps/gke/remote-state.tf (add this):
   154→data "terraform_remote_state" "waf" {
   155→  backend   = "gcs"
   156→  workspace = terraform.workspace  # reads policy for current workspace
   157→  config = {
   158→    bucket = "liftit-tf-state"
   159→    prefix = "sec/waf"
   160→  }
   161→}
   162→```
   163→
   164→```hcl
   165→# In apps/gke/load-balancer.tf:
   166→module "gke-apps-load-balancer" {
   167→  ...
   168→  cloud_armor_policy = data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.waf_policy_name
   169→}
   170→```
   171→
   172→The `cloud_armor_policy` variable in `tf-modules//load-balancer` is typed as `string` and is passed directly to `google_compute_backend_service.security_policy`. GCP accepts the policy **name** (not full self_link) when the backend service is in the same project as the policy. Since each workspace maps to one GCP project and sec/waf deploys a policy per workspace, the policy for workspace `qa` lives in `security-454414`, while GKE backends live in `qa-apps-454414` — **these are different projects**.
   173→
   174→This means even the name-based reference is cross-project. The self_link format for cross-project reference is:
   175→
   176→```
   177→https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/security-454414/global/securityPolicies/liftit-waf-qa
   178→```
   179→
   180→Or in resource ID format:
   181→```
   182→projects/security-454414/global/securityPolicies/liftit-waf-qa
   183→```
   184→
   185→**This confirms the cross-project limitation applies and Cloud Armor Enterprise is required for the centralized-in-sec approach.** The practical alternative for this milestone is to deploy the WAF policy in the same project as the load balancer (i.e., in qa/staging/prod projects, not sec).
   186→
   187→### Revised Architecture for This Milestone
   188→
   189→Deploy WAF policy per-environment in the environment's own project (not in sec):
   190→
   191→| Workspace | GCP Project | Policy Name | Where deployed |
   192→|-----------|-------------|-------------|----------------|
   193→| qa | qa-apps-454414 | liftit-waf-qa | apps/gke workspace=qa OR a new waf module in qa |
   194→| bi | liftit-bi | liftit-waf-bi | bi/apps workspace=bi |
   195→| sha | shared-016 | liftit-waf-sha | common/apps workspace=sha |
   196→
   197→The sec/waf module retains the policy for any resources within the sec project. This pattern avoids Enterprise costs while achieving the same rule consistency through shared Terraform module code.
   198→
   199→---
   200→
   201→## Supporting Libraries / Resources
   202→
   203→| Resource | Version | Purpose | When to Use |
   204→|----------|---------|---------|-------------|
   205→| `google_compute_security_policy_rule` | Google Provider ~> 7.0 | Standalone rule management (separate from policy) | Use when adding exclusion rules that can't be expressed via the existing waf module's `rules` map |
   206→| `data.google_compute_security_policy` | Google Provider ~> 7.0 | Read existing policy attributes | Use to read self_link from same-project policy for backend service attachment |
   207→| `terraform_remote_state` (sec/waf) | Terraform ~> 1.14 | Read waf_policy_name across modules | Use in each LB module to wire up the policy |
   208→
   209→### Cloud Armor Logging (Required for Analysis)
   210→
   211→WAF logs appear in Cloud Logging under `resource.type="http_load_balancer"`. No separate Terraform resource required — Cloud Armor automatically logs to Cloud Logging when attached to an external HTTPS LB. Filter for preview violations:
   212→
   213→```
   214→resource.type="http_load_balancer"
   215→jsonPayload.enforcedSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"
   216→jsonPayload.enforcedSecurityPolicy.preconfiguredExprIds!=""
   217→```
   218→
   219→Or for preview-only (not enforced):
   220→```
   221→jsonPayload.previewSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"
   222→```
   223→
   224→---
   225→
   226→## Development Tools
   227→
   228→| Tool | Purpose | Notes |
   229→|------|---------|-------|
   230→| `gcloud compute security-policies describe` | Inspect deployed policy | Use to verify rule state after `terraform apply` |
   231→| `gcloud compute security-policies list-preconfigured-expression-sets` | List available rule sets and IDs | Use to get exact signature IDs for opt_out tuning |
   232→| Cloud Logging (Log Explorer) | Analyze preview violations | Filter by `jsonPayload.previewSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"` |
   233→| `gcloud logging read` | Programmatic log analysis | Pipe to jq to count violations per rule ID per service |
   234→
   235→---
   236→
   237→## What NOT to Use
   238→
   239→| Avoid | Why | Use Instead |
   240→|-------|-----|-------------|
   241→| `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr()` | Deprecated; only inspects request headers, not body; no sensitivity parameter | `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf()` with explicit sensitivity level |
   242→| Cloud Armor Enterprise (for this milestone) | $200+/month cost; cross-project referencing benefit doesn't justify cost when same-project deployment achieves the same result | Deploy policy in the same project as the LB |
   243→| `google_compute_security_policy` `adaptive_protection_config` block | Adaptive Protection requires Enterprise enrollment; out of scope per PROJECT.md | Not needed for OWASP rule activation milestone |
   244→| Hierarchical security policies | Requires Enterprise; limited Terraform support; org/folder level not project | Per-environment policies managed by Terraform |
   245→| `sqli-stable` / `xss-stable` (CRS 3.0 versions) | CRS 3.0 lacks Java/NodeJS coverage; v33 is recommended by Google | `sqli-v33-stable`, `xss-v33-stable`, etc. |
   246→| v33-canary variants | Newer signatures, may introduce false positives; upgrade is separate milestone scope | Keep v33-stable for current milestone |
   247→| `google_compute_security_policy.advanced_options_config` (body inspection size) | Body inspection up to 64kB now GA, but current module does not expose this; adds complexity without clear benefit for this milestone | Add after QA validation confirms base rules work |
   248→
   249→---
   250→
   251→## Stack Patterns by Variant
   252→
   253→**If backend service is in the same GCP project as the security policy:**
   254→- Use policy name directly: `cloud_armor_policy = "liftit-waf-qa"`
   255→- Or read via remote state: `data.terraform_remote_state.waf.outputs.waf_policy_name`
   256→- No Enterprise required
   257→
   258→**If backend service is in a different GCP project than the security policy:**
   259→- Requires Cloud Armor Enterprise Annual for both projects
   260→- Full self_link format: `REDACTED`
   261→- Not recommended for this milestone
   262→
   263→**If a service needs WAF exclusions (high false-positive risk):**
   264→- Add `preconfigured_waf_config` block to the specific `google_compute_security_policy_rule`
   265→- Keep the rule in preview while tuning
   266→- Activate only after zero false positives confirmed in QA logs
   267→
   268→**If WAF policy needs to cover backend buckets (frontends):**
   269→- Cloud Armor **does NOT apply** to `google_compute_backend_bucket` resources
   270→- Only `google_compute_backend_service` supports `security_policy`
   271→- Frontend static sites (GCS buckets behind LB) cannot be protected by Cloud Armor WAF rules
   272→- Rate limiting and IP-based rules on the URL map level require `google_compute_security_policy` on the backend service type
   273→
   274→---
   275→
   276→## Version Compatibility
   277→
   278→| Component | Version | Compatibility Note |
   279→|-----------|---------|-------------------|
   280→| Terraform | `~> 1.14` | Compatible with all resources listed |
   281→| Google Provider | `~> 7.0` | `google_compute_security_policy_rule` with `preconfigured_waf_config` is fully supported |
   282→| `google_compute_security_policy_rule` | Stable in google provider ≥ 4.58 | `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusion block GA as of provider ~> 5.x |
   283→| `tf-modules//waf` | Current version | Does NOT expose `preconfigured_waf_config` — exclusions require direct `google_compute_security_policy_rule` resources outside the module OR module extension |
   284→| `tf-modules//load-balancer` | Current version | `cloud_armor_policy` variable is `string`, accepts policy name or full resource URL |
   285→
   286→---
   287→
   288→## Sources
   289→
   290→- [Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/waf-rules) — Rule set names, CRS versions, evaluatePreconfiguredWaf syntax (HIGH confidence)
   291→- [Tune Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/rule-tuning) — Sensitivity levels, opt_out/opt_in, exclusion block structure (HIGH confidence)
   292→- [Cloud Armor rules language reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/rules-language-reference) — evaluatePreconfiguredExpr deprecation confirmed, evaluatePreconfiguredWaf signature (HIGH confidence)
   293→- [Cloud Armor Enterprise overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/armor-enterprise-overview) — Cross-project referencing requires Enterprise enrollment (HIGH confidence — critical constraint)
   294→- [Configure hierarchical security policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/hierarchical-policies-using) — Org/folder level policies, association mechanism (MEDIUM confidence)
   295→- [Cloud Armor release notes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/release-notes) — No versions beyond v33-stable as of Feb 2026; cve-canary updated Dec 2025 (HIGH confidence)
   296→- [google_compute_security_policy Terraform docs](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-google/blob/main/website/docs/r/compute_security_policy.html.markdown) — Resource attributes, preconfigured_waf_config schema (HIGH confidence)
   297→- Direct codebase inspection: `sec/waf/waf.tf`, `sec/waf/.terraform/modules/cloud_armor/waf/main.tf`, `sec/waf/.terraform/modules/cloud_armor/load-balancer/variables.tf` — Existing implementation, current gaps (HIGH confidence)
   298→
   299→---
   300→
   301→*Stack research for: Cloud Armor WAF production deployment on Liftit GCP infrastructure*
   302→*Researched: 2026-02-24*
