1→# Pitfalls Research
     2→
     3→**Domain:** Cloud Armor WAF activation on existing multi-project GCP infrastructure
     4→**Researched:** 2026-02-24
     5→**Confidence:** HIGH (official Google documentation) / MEDIUM (community patterns) / LOW (inferred from infrastructure analysis)
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Critical Pitfalls
    10→
    11→### Pitfall 1: Cross-Project Policy Attachment Is Not Straightforward
    12→
    13→**What goes wrong:**
    14→The planned architecture centralize the WAF policy in the `sec` project (security-454414) and reference it from load balancers in `qa`, `prod`, `bi`, and `sha` projects. Cloud Armor security policies are project-scoped resources. A `google_compute_backend_service` in project `qa-apps-454414` cannot attach a `google_compute_security_policy` that lives in `security-454414` using a simple name reference. Only self_links work — and even self_links require the backend service's project to have authorization to use the foreign policy. Cross-project service referencing for Cloud Armor explicitly requires Cloud Armor Enterprise enrollment for both projects under the same billing account.
    15→
    16→**Why it happens:**
    17→The architecture decision to centralize the policy in `sec` follows the same pattern used for KMS (centralized in `sec`), but KMS cross-project reference is a first-class GCP feature. Cloud Armor cross-project policy reference is not — it is an Enterprise tier feature. The existing `sec/waf/outputs.tf` only exports `waf_policy_name` (a string name), not the `self_link`. Even if the self_link were exported via remote state, attaching it to a backend service in a different project would fail without Enterprise enrollment.
    18→
    19→**How to avoid:**
    20→Two viable options exist:
    21→
    22→Option A — Per-project policies (no Enterprise required): Keep the existing pattern of one policy per workspace. The `sec/waf` module already creates `liftit-waf-${workspace}`. Each workspace's load balancer references its own local policy. Use Terraform module composition to keep rules DRY. This is the current architecture and requires zero cross-project IAM changes.
    23→
    24→Option B — Hierarchical policy (Enterprise auto-enrolled): Use `google_compute_organization_security_policy` instead of `google_compute_security_policy`. Hierarchical policies attach at org/folder level and automatically cover all projects below. This triggers automatic Cloud Armor Enterprise Paygo enrollment — verify cost implications before choosing this path.
    25→
    26→Do NOT assume a policy self_link from the `sec` project can be passed to a `google_compute_backend_service` in the `qa` project without Enterprise.
    27→
    28→**Warning signs:**
    29→- Terraform plan shows `google_compute_backend_service.security_policy` accepting a self_link from a different project
    30→- No Cloud Armor Enterprise subscription visible in billing
    31→- Apply succeeds but security policy is not actually enforced (no logs appear)
    32→
    33→**Phase to address:**
    34→Phase 1 (Architecture Decision). This must be resolved before any Terraform code is written. Validate the cross-project approach with a minimal test: create a policy in `sec`, attempt to attach it to a backend service in `qa` via self_link, and observe whether it applies.
    35→
    36→---
    37→
    38→### Pitfall 2: Method Enforcement Rule Blocks All REST API Traffic
    39→
    40→**What goes wrong:**
    41→Rule `1080` uses `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('methodenforcement-v33-stable')`. The OWASP CRS method enforcement ruleset (rule owasp-crs-v030301-id911100) defines an allowed methods list. By default, only GET, HEAD, POST, and OPTIONS pass. PUT, DELETE, and PATCH are blocked. Every microservice in the GKE cluster uses standard REST conventions with PUT, DELETE, and PATCH. When this rule is activated (preview=false), all update/delete REST operations across all 35+ microservices will return 403.
    42→
    43→**Why it happens:**
    44→The OWASP CRS method enforcement rule was designed for traditional web applications that only use GET and POST. Modern REST APIs universally use PUT/PATCH/DELETE. Cloud Armor does not expose the CRS configuration option to extend the allowed methods list — unlike self-hosted ModSecurity. The only workaround is path-based exclusions or disabling the rule entirely.
    45→
    46→**How to avoid:**
    47→Either disable the method enforcement rule entirely (recommended for a REST microservices architecture), or create explicit allow rules before rule `1080` for each HTTP method used. Given the API-centric nature of all Liftit services, the method enforcement rule provides near-zero value and maximum false positive risk. The correct decision is to exclude PUT, DELETE, and PATCH globally or drop this rule from the active set.
    48→
    49→Log analysis during preview mode will show volume: expect 100% of PUT/PATCH/DELETE requests to appear as would-be violations.
    50→
    51→**Warning signs:**
    52→- During preview mode analysis, rule 1080 appears in every API update/delete operation log entry
    53→- Any endpoint with standard CRUD patterns shows violations against this rule
    54→
    55→**Phase to address:**
    56→Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis). When analyzing preview logs, rule 1080 will be the most frequently triggered rule by volume. Flag it immediately for exclusion or removal before activation.
    57→
    58→---
    59→
    60→### Pitfall 3: Superset and Metabase Will Be Completely Broken by SQLi Rules
    61→
    62→**What goes wrong:**
    63→Superset and Metabase are SQL query builder tools. Their core function is to transmit raw SQL queries from the browser to the backend via HTTP POST/PUT request bodies. The SQLi rule (`1030`, `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sqli-v33-stable')`) will detect these legitimate SQL payloads as SQL injection attacks and block them. Every chart creation, dashboard query, and dataset exploration operation will return 403.
    64→
    65→The `json-sqli-canary` rule (`1160`) compounds this: Superset's API uses JSON request bodies containing SQL queries, meaning every API call that includes a SQL query in JSON format triggers this rule too.
    66→
    67→**Why it happens:**
    68→WAF SQLi detection operates on pattern matching, not context. A `SELECT orders.id, customers.name FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id` payload is indistinguishable from SQL injection to a pattern-matching WAF. Metabase's `/api/card` endpoint (PUT and POST) and Superset's `/api/v1/chart/` and `/api/v1/dataset/` endpoints all send raw SQL in request bodies.
    69→
    70→**How to avoid:**
    71→Add request path exclusions for Superset and Metabase backend endpoints from the SQLi rules before activation. Both tools use prepared statements internally, making external SQLi rules redundant for their traffic.
    72→
    73→Terraform exclusion pattern:
    74→```hcl
    75→preconfigured_waf_config {
    76→  exclusion {
    77→    target_rule_set = "sqli-v33-stable"
    78→    request_uri {
    79→      op    = "STARTS_WITH"
    80→      value = "/api/"
    81→    }
    82→  }
    83→}
    84→```
    85→
    86→The bi-apps LB hosts both Metabase and Superset. The Superset UI also allows custom SQL, meaning the exclusion needs to cover the entire `/api/` path tree for both applications.
    87→
    88→**Warning signs:**
    89→- Rule 1030 and 1160 appear in preview logs for ALL Superset and Metabase traffic that involves chart creation or SQL editing
    90→
    91→**Phase to address:**
    92→Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis). Superset and Metabase endpoints must be catalogued and excluded from SQLi rules before activation. This is a guaranteed false positive, not a maybe.
    93→
    94→---
    95→
    96→### Pitfall 4: Keycloak Auth Flows Trigger Multiple WAF Rules Simultaneously
    97→
    98→**What goes wrong:**
    99→Keycloak generates complex authentication flows involving:
   100→- Long JWT access tokens in Authorization headers (may trigger XSS or RCE pattern detection)
   101→- Base64-encoded session data in cookies (may trigger sessionfixation rules)
   102→- PKCE code_challenge parameters with high-entropy strings (may trigger scanner detection)
   103→- Special characters in password fields (`!@#$%^&*`) that trigger SQLi or XSS patterns
   104→- SAML assertion payloads in POST bodies that contain XML with encoded characters
   105→
   106→Users attempting login with complex passwords or using SAML-based SSO may receive 403 responses. Since Keycloak is the authentication gateway for the entire platform, blocking it effectively locks out all users.
   107→
   108→**Why it happens:**
   109→The Keycloak community has documented (GitHub Discussion #35586) that there is "no perfect solution" for WAF compatibility — every deployment requires custom exclusion tuning. The Keycloak login flow sends credentials in POST body fields that WAF rules interpret as potential attacks. Session fixation rules are particularly problematic because Keycloak deliberately manages session tokens across redirects (which is what session fixation protection is designed to prevent, but Keycloak's implementation is legitimate).
   110→
   111→**How to avoid:**
   112→Apply path-based exclusions to all Keycloak endpoints before activation:
   113→- `/auth/realms/*/protocol/openid-connect/token` (token endpoint)
   114→- `/auth/realms/*/protocol/openid-connect/auth` (authorization endpoint)
   115→- `/auth/admin/*` (admin console)
   116→- `/auth/realms/*/login-actions/*` (login flows)
   117→
   118→Test specifically with: password login using special characters, SAML SSO flows, token refresh operations, and admin console access.
   119→
   120→**Warning signs:**
   121→- Any preview log entry for `keycloak.*` hostnames showing violations against sessionfixation, xss, or sqli rules
   122→- Rule 1120 (sessionfixation) appearing frequently for `/auth/` paths
   123→
   124→**Phase to address:**
   125→Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis) with dedicated Keycloak test scenario. Phase 3 (Fine-tuning) for exclusion configuration.
   126→
   127→---
   128→
   129→### Pitfall 5: Logging Is Not Enabled by Default — Silent Failures
   130→
   131→**What goes wrong:**
   132→Cloud Armor request logging is disabled by default for all backend services. The WAF can be attached to a load balancer in preview mode and appear to be working — the Terraform apply succeeds, the policy is associated — but zero logs are generated. There is no visibility into what the WAF is evaluating, no evidence of what would be blocked, and no ability to detect false positives. The entire preview phase analysis produces nothing.
   133→
   134→**Why it happens:**
   135→GCP disables backend service logging by default to avoid billing surprises. Engineers attaching the WAF policy assume logging is part of the policy, not the backend service. The `google_compute_backend_service` resource has a separate `log_config` block that defaults to disabled. This is separate from Cloud Armor verbose logging.
   136→
   137→**How to avoid:**
   138→Explicitly enable logging on every backend service that has the WAF policy attached. In the load-balancer module, ensure `log_config { enable = true, sample_rate = 1.0 }` is set during the analysis phase. Reduce sample_rate to 0.1 after tuning is complete if log volume is a concern.
   139→
   140→The critical log filter for false positive detection:
   141→```
   142→resource.type="http_load_balancer"
   143→jsonPayload.enforcedSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"
   144→```
   145→
   146→For preview mode violations (would-have-been-blocked):
   147→```
   148→resource.type="http_load_balancer"
   149→jsonPayload.previewSecurityPolicy.outcome="DENY"
   150→```
   151→
   152→**Warning signs:**
   153→- No Cloud Armor log entries in Cloud Logging after policy attachment
   154→- The `log_config` block is absent from the backend service Terraform resource
   155→
   156→**Phase to address:**
   157→Phase 1 (Policy Attachment). Enable logging as part of the same Terraform apply that attaches the WAF policy. Never attach a WAF policy without logging enabled.
   158→
   159→---
   160→
   161→### Pitfall 6: Rate Limiting Rule Blocks Cloud Scheduler Jobs
   162→
   163→**What goes wrong:**
   164→Rule `1170` bans IPs exceeding 1000 req/min (with a ban threshold of 2000 req/min for 5 minutes). Cloud Scheduler jobs call microservice endpoints on scheduled intervals. Multiple scheduler jobs calling the same service in a burst — or a single high-frequency job like `reenviar-ordenes-pendientes-pricesmart` (every 5 minutes), `resync_services_lms_to_tms` (every 15 minutes), or `advances-payment-request-confirm` (every 15 minutes) — originate from Google Cloud infrastructure IPs that are shared and not predictable in advance. A scheduled batch spike can trigger the rate ban, causing a 5-minute service blackout for all traffic from the affected IP range.
   165→
   166→**Why it happens:**
   167→Cloud Scheduler requests originate from Google's shared infrastructure, not from dedicated static IPs. The source IP of a scheduler job cannot be whitelisted because it is not fixed. During integration tests or batch runs, multiple scheduler jobs executing in parallel from the same underlying Google infrastructure IP can collectively exceed the 1000 req/min threshold, triggering the ban.
   168→
   169→The existing IP whitelist (rule 1000) only includes the NAT gateway IPs for each workspace — not the scheduler's originating IPs.
   170→
   171→**How to avoid:**
   172→Keep rule 1170 (rate limit) in preview mode longer than other rules. Independently analyze rate-limit preview log entries to understand whether Google Scheduler source IPs appear in violation logs. Consider using `THROTTLE` action instead of `rate_based_ban` — throttle limits the rate without banning the source, which prevents legitimate services from being locked out entirely.
   173→
   174→Alternatively, add a CIDR allowlist for Google's health check and scheduler IP ranges (documented by Google) with higher priority than rule 1170.
   175→
   176→**Warning signs:**
   177→- Preview logs showing rule 1170 triggered by `googleapis.com` user-agents or scheduler service accounts
   178→- 403 responses appearing for scheduled jobs in Cloud Scheduler execution history
   179→
   180→**Phase to address:**
   181→Phase 3 (Fine-tuning). Rate limit rule analysis requires traffic pattern data from preview logs. Validate separately from OWASP rules.
   182→
   183→---
   184→
   185→### Pitfall 7: File Upload Endpoints Bypassed By the 8KB Body Inspection Limit
   186→
   187→**What goes wrong:**
   188→Cloud Armor only inspects the first 8,192 bytes of HTTP POST/PUT request bodies. Excel-loader, lms-excel-loader, and docscan-service handle large file uploads (Excel files, scanned documents) that are far larger than 8KB. Cloud Armor scans only the first 8KB and then passes the rest through unchecked — meaning a malicious payload embedded after the 8KB mark in a multi-part upload bypasses all WAF inspection. This creates a security gap that is invisible unless explicitly addressed.
   189→
   190→**Why it happens:**
   191→This is a documented GCP WAF architecture limitation, not a configuration error. The design assumption is that WAF inspection applies to request metadata and small payloads, not large binary file uploads. The documentation notes this default pass-through behavior explicitly.
   192→
   193→**How to avoid:**
   194→Add a custom Cloud Armor rule that blocks requests where `Content-Length > 8192` unless the request is to an explicitly allowed upload endpoint. For the known upload endpoints (excel-loader, lms-excel-loader, docscan-service), add path-specific rules that allow large payloads but flag them for application-level validation.
   195→
   196→Example rule (to be added to waf.tf):
   197→```hcl
   198→"900" = {
   199→  action      = "deny(403)"
   200→  description = "Block oversized requests except on upload endpoints"
   201→  preview     = true
   202→  expr        = "int(request.headers['content-length']) > 8192 && !request.path.matches('/upload/.*') && !request.path.matches('/api/upload.*')"
   203→}
   204→```
   205→
   206→This pitfall is not about false positives — it is about a security gap that the WAF appears to close but does not.
   207→
   208→**Warning signs:**
   209→- No custom Content-Length rule in the policy
   210→- File upload endpoints not explicitly listed in WAF exclusion documentation
   211→
   212→**Phase to address:**
   213→Phase 2 (Endpoint Analysis). Document all file upload endpoints and their expected payload sizes. Phase 3 (Fine-tuning) to add the Content-Length protection rule.
   214→
   215→---
   216→
   217→### Pitfall 8: Activating Rules Individually Without Incremental Traffic Analysis
   218→
   219→**What goes wrong:**
   220→All 17 OWASP rules are currently in preview mode. The naive activation path is to flip all `preview = false` in one apply. This creates an immediately undebuggable situation: when users start getting 403 errors, there is no way to determine which of the 17 rules is responsible without examining individual log entries. Even with logs enabled, multiple rules may fire simultaneously on the same request, complicating root cause analysis.
   221→
   222→**Why it happens:**
   223→It is tempting to treat preview-to-active as a single toggle since all the rules exist. The assumption is "we checked the logs, it looks fine." But preview log analysis at low traffic volume may miss edge cases that appear at production load or with specific user workflows.
   224→
   225→**How to avoid:**
   226→Activate rules one at a time or in logical groups, with a 24-48 hour monitoring window between each activation. Suggested activation order (least risky to most risky for this infrastructure):
   227→
   228→1. Scanner detection (1090) — lowest false positive rate for API services
   229→2. LFI (1050), RFI (1070) — rarely triggered by legitimate REST traffic
   230→3. RCE (1060) — low risk for standard application payloads
   231→4. Java (1130), NodeJS (1140) — relevant to tech stack but focused signatures
   232→5. Protocol attacks (1100) — low false positive for standard HTTP/HTTPS
   233→6. XSS (1040) — moderate risk; inspect carefully for admin panel traffic
   234→7. Session fixation (1120) — activate only after Keycloak exclusions are confirmed
   235→8. SQLi (1030), JSON-SQLi (1160) — activate only after BI tool exclusions confirmed
   236→9. Method enforcement (1080) — requires careful review; likely disable for REST APIs
   237→10. Rate limiting (1170) — activate last; validate scheduler traffic first
   238→
   239→**Warning signs:**
   240→- Terraform plan shows all rules switching to `preview = false` in one change
   241→- No documented per-rule activation schedule in the milestone plan
   242→
   243→**Phase to address:**
   244→Phase 4 (Activation). The phase must explicitly define an incremental activation sequence, not a bulk toggle.
   245→
   246→---
   247→
   248→## Technical Debt Patterns
   249→
   250→| Shortcut | Immediate Benefit | Long-term Cost | When Acceptable |
   251→|----------|-------------------|----------------|-----------------|
   252→| Activate all rules simultaneously | Faster to production-active state | Undebuggable false positives; impossible to isolate which rule caused which error | Never |
   253→| Skip logging enablement | Lower Cloud Logging costs | No visibility into WAF behavior; blind WAF deployment | Never |
   254→| Keep method enforcement rule active | Appears more "complete" coverage | Blocks all PUT/DELETE/PATCH REST traffic; major outage | Never for REST API infrastructure |
   255→| Same policy for BI tools and microservices | Simpler Terraform | SQLi rules must be disabled globally because of Superset/Metabase, weakening protection for other services | Only if separate LBs/policies are not feasible |
   256→| Skip cross-project architecture validation | Faster initial implementation | Discover Enterprise tier requirement mid-milestone; forced architecture change under time pressure | Never |
   257→| Use `cve-canary` without version pinning | Always current CVE coverage | Rule set can change without notice, introducing new false positives unexpectedly | Never in production without a review gate |
   258→
   259→---
   260→
   261→## Integration Gotchas
   262→
   263→| Integration | Common Mistake | Correct Approach |
   264→|-------------|----------------|------------------|
   265→| Keycloak | Applying WAF rules to all `/auth/` paths without exclusions | Add per-path exclusions for token endpoint, login-actions, and admin console before activation |
   266→| Kong API Gateway | Assuming WAF inspection happens at the Kong layer | WAF operates at the LB layer before Kong; all requests through `gateway-*.liftit-sandbox.com` are inspected at the L7 LB, not at Kong itself |
   267→| Superset / Metabase | Applying SQLi rules without path exclusions | Exclude `/api/` paths on the bi-apps LB from sqli and json-sqli rules before activation |
   268→| Cloud Scheduler | Not accounting for scheduler source IPs in rate limit allowlist | Analyze scheduler source IPs from preview logs; consider THROTTLE instead of rate_based_ban |
   269→| Django admin (support-administration, backoffice-api) | Django CSRF tokens in POST bodies triggering XSS or session fixation rules | Add path exclusions for `/admin/` and login endpoints; verify Django's csrftoken cookie does not trigger sessionfixation rules |
   270→| Excel/document file uploads | Assuming WAF inspects entire file content | Cloud Armor only inspects first 8KB; add Content-Length protection rules for upload endpoints |
   271→| Cloud Run services | `domain-map.tf` has `cloud_armor_policy = null` — Cloud Run domain mappings do not use the same backend service mechanism | Cloud Run domain mappings managed by `apps/cloudrun` use `google_cloud_run_domain_mapping`, not an LB backend service; Cloud Armor cannot be attached directly to Cloud Run domain mappings in this manner |
   272→
   273→---
   274→
   275→## Performance Traps
   276→
   277→| Trap | Symptoms | Prevention | When It Breaks |
   278→|------|----------|------------|----------------|
   279→| Rate limiting set too low for batch operations | Scheduler jobs return 403 during batch runs; services intermittently unavailable | Monitor rate limit preview logs for 48 hours including batch windows before activation | Immediately upon activation if 30+ scheduler jobs run concurrently |
   280→| Verbose logging enabled in production long-term | Cloud Logging costs spike; PII (tokens, passwords) appears in logs | Enable verbose logging only during tuning; disable after exclusions are confirmed | Continuously; costs accumulate daily |
   281→| Full log sampling (sample_rate=1.0) kept post-tuning | High Cloud Logging ingestion costs for high-traffic services | Reduce to 0.1 after tuning is complete | At scale; 35+ microservices with full logging is expensive |
   282→| Single security policy for all 7 LBs | BI tool exclusions (SQLi disabled) applied globally, weakening protection for core microservices | Use separate policy or per-backend exclusions; the bi-apps LB needs different tuning than gke-apps LB | Not a performance trap but a security degradation that is invisible |
   283→
   284→---
   285→
   286→## Security Mistakes
   287→
   288→| Mistake | Risk | Prevention |
   289→|---------|------|------------|
   290→| Activating WAF without endpoint-specific exclusions for Superset/Metabase | 100% of SQL query builder operations blocked | Catalogue and exclude BI tool API endpoints from SQLi rules before activation |
   291→| Relying solely on WAF for file upload security | Malicious payloads embedded after 8KB bypass all WAF inspection | Add Content-Length rule; implement application-level validation in upload services |
   292→| Treating preview mode as "safe to ignore" | Preview logs contain the only evidence of what will break before activation; ignoring them means blind activation | Analyze every preview log entry; build a false positive register before any rule goes active |
   293→| Not outputting policy `self_link` from `sec/waf` | Cannot reference policy from other modules even if cross-project is validated | Add `waf_policy_self_link` output to `sec/waf/outputs.tf` regardless of architecture choice |
   294→| User-agent blocking (rule 1010) blocking monitoring tools | GoogleStackdriverMonitoring appears in the user-agent deny list (rule 1020 denies it) — the description says "Permitir" but the action is "deny(403)" | Rule 1020 as written BLOCKS uptime checks, not allows them. This is a configuration bug: the description and action contradict each other. Fix rule 1020 action to "allow" before activating |
   295→
   296→---
   297→
   298→## "Looks Done But Isn't" Checklist
   299→
   300→- [ ] **Logging enabled**: `log_config { enable = true }` is set on every backend service — not just the policy attached. Verify in GCP Console that log entries appear after policy attachment.
   301→- [ ] **Rule 1020 corrected**: The Stackdriver monitoring rule has `action = "deny(403)"` with a description that says "Permitir" (allow). This is a bug. Verify the intended behavior and fix before activating.
   302→- [ ] **Cross-project attachment validated**: Confirm whether the centralized `sec` policy can attach to backends in `qa` project — do not assume; test with a real apply to a single non-critical backend service.
   303→- [ ] **Method enforcement reviewed**: Confirm all HTTP methods used by GKE microservices are accounted for. PUT, DELETE, PATCH will be blocked by rule 1080.
   304→- [ ] **BI tool exclusions documented**: Superset and Metabase SQLi exclusions are specified per endpoint path in Terraform before rule 1030 goes active.
   305→- [ ] **Keycloak test coverage**: Authentication flows with special-character passwords, SAML SSO, and token refresh have all been tested in preview logs before activation.
   306→- [ ] **Rate limit threshold validated**: 1000 req/min per IP has been verified against actual peak traffic metrics for the highest-volume services (tms-api, tracking-service, kong).
   307→- [ ] **Cloud Run WAF gap acknowledged**: `apps/cloudrun` domain mappings cannot attach Cloud Armor; these services remain unprotected at the WAF layer regardless of this milestone.
   308→- [ ] **8KB Content-Length rule added**: A custom rule blocking oversized requests to non-upload endpoints is added to the policy.
   309→- [ ] **Activation sequence documented**: Each rule's activation is scheduled individually, not as a bulk toggle.
   310→
   311→---
   312→
   313→## Recovery Strategies
   314→
   315→| Pitfall | Recovery Cost | Recovery Steps |
   316→|---------|---------------|----------------|
   317→| Wrong rule blocks production traffic after activation | HIGH | Set `preview = true` for the offending rule in Terraform; apply immediately; Terraform apply propagates in ~2 minutes; analyze logs to identify excluded paths |
   318→| Rate ban locks out legitimate IPs | MEDIUM | Add the banned IP/range to the IP whitelist (rule 1000) with priority lower than 1000 but higher than 1170; ban expires in 300 seconds automatically |
   319→| Cross-project attachment fails at apply time | MEDIUM | Fall back to per-project policy pattern; `sec/waf` already creates per-workspace policies; re-enable them in the target workspace |
   320→| Superset/Metabase completely down after SQLi activation | HIGH | Immediately set rule 1030 and 1160 back to `preview = true`; add path exclusions for `/api/` on the bi-apps LB; re-activate with exclusions |
   321→| Logging not enabled — no data for analysis | LOW | Enable `log_config` on backend service; wait 30-60 minutes for data to appear; preview analysis must restart from baseline |
   322→| Rule 1020 blocks Stackdriver uptime checks | MEDIUM | Fix action from `deny(403)` to `allow` in waf.tf; apply; uptime checks resume immediately |
   323→
   324→---
   325→
   326→## Pitfall-to-Phase Mapping
   327→
   328→| Pitfall | Prevention Phase | Verification |
   329→|---------|------------------|--------------|
   330→| Cross-project policy attachment | Phase 1: Architecture validation | Test apply of policy self_link to one QA backend service; check if enforcement appears in logs |
   331→| Method enforcement breaks REST APIs | Phase 2: Endpoint analysis | Review preview logs for rule 1080; count PUT/DELETE/PATCH violation volume |
   332→| Superset/Metabase SQLi false positives | Phase 2: BI tool endpoint catalogue | Zero rule 1030/1160 violations for normal BI workflows in preview logs |
   333→| Keycloak auth flow false positives | Phase 2: Auth flow testing | Full Keycloak login test suite produces zero violations in preview logs |
   334→| Logging not enabled | Phase 1: Policy attachment | Cloud Logging shows entries within 5 minutes of policy attach |
   335→| Rate limiting blocks schedulers | Phase 2/3: Rate limit analysis | No rule 1170 violations from Google Cloud Scheduler source IPs in 48-hour preview window |
   336→| 8KB file upload bypass | Phase 3: Fine-tuning | Content-Length rule added and tested with test upload exceeding 8KB |
   337→| Bulk rule activation | Phase 4: Incremental activation | Each rule activated individually; 24-hour monitoring window documented between activations |
   338→| Rule 1020 config bug | Phase 1: Policy audit | Rule 1020 action verified correct before any LB attachment |
   339→
   340→---
   341→
   342→## Phase-Specific Warnings
   343→
   344→| Phase Topic | Likely Pitfall | Mitigation |
   345→|-------------|---------------|------------|
   346→| Centralizing policy in sec project | Cross-project attachment requires Enterprise or architecture change | Validate attachment feasibility before committing to architecture |
   347→| Attaching to bi-apps LB (Superset/Metabase) | SQLi rules will block all chart/query operations | Pre-define path exclusions in waf.tf before setting preview=false for rules 1030/1160 |
   348→| Attaching to gke-apps LB (35+ microservices) | Method enforcement will block REST operations; rate limit may fire during batch | Keep rules 1080 and 1170 in preview longest; analyze per-service violation volume |
   349→| Activating sessionfixation rule (1120) | Keycloak uses cross-redirect session management that looks like fixation | Require Keycloak endpoint exclusions to be merged before this rule goes active |
   350→| Activating on keycloak backend | Auth outage blocks all users | Test separately with health-check validation; have rollback committed before applying |
   351→| Activating on Kong gateway backend | Kong proxies to all downstream services; a false positive here blocks everything routed through Kong | Activate on Kong last; it must be the final service to get active WAF enforcement |
   352→
   353→---
   354→

# Project Research Summary

**Project:** Cloud Armor WAF — OWASP Rules Activation & Policy Attachment
**Domain:** GCP Cloud Armor WAF deployment on multi-project Terraform infrastructure
**Researched:** 2026-02-24
**Confidence:** HIGH

## Executive Summary

This milestone activates Google Cloud Armor OWASP WAF rules — already deployed in preview mode via `sec/waf` — by attaching the security policy to all load balancers and systematically promoting rules from preview to enforcement. The critical architectural constraint is that Cloud Armor security policies are project-scoped: a policy created in `security-454414` (sec workspace) cannot be attached to backend services in `qa-apps-454414`, `prod-apps-454414`, `liftit-bi`, or `shared-016` without Cloud Armor Enterprise enrollment ($200+/month/project). The recommended architecture is to use multi-provider aliases in `sec/waf` to deploy identical policies into each target project from a single Terraform run, with each LB reading the policy name via remote state. This avoids Enterprise costs while maintaining centralized rule management.

The WAF activation path must be incremental and analysis-driven. Certain services will generate guaranteed false positives at any sensitivity level: Superset and Metabase (SQL query builder traffic triggers SQLi rules), Keycloak (JWT tokens and session management trigger XSS and session fixation rules), and file upload services (multipart binary data triggers LFI/RFI rules). These exclusions must be in place before any rule is promoted from preview to enforce. The method enforcement rule (1080) must be reviewed as a probable disable-candidate — it blocks PUT/DELETE/PATCH by default, which breaks all REST API traffic across 35+ microservices. A configuration bug in rule 1020 also requires immediate correction: the rule description says "allow" but the action is `deny(403)`, which would block Stackdriver uptime checks upon enforcement.

The recommended approach is a four-phase rollout: (1) architecture validation and policy fix-up, (2) policy deployment and LB attachment in preview mode with verbose logging, (3) endpoint analysis using Cloud Logging preview-deny data to build per-service exclusions, and (4) incremental rule-by-rule activation with 24-hour monitoring windows between each promotion. No bulk activation. Cloud Run services (`apps/cloudrun`) cannot receive WAF protection through this mechanism — Cloud Armor only attaches to `google_compute_backend_service`, not to Cloud Run domain mappings.

---

## Key Findings

### Recommended Stack

The existing stack requires no version changes. Terraform `~> 1.14` and Google Provider `~> 7.0` fully support all required resources including `google_compute_security_policy_rule` with `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusion blocks. All 14 OWASP rule sets run at CRS 3.3 stable (`-v33-stable`), which is the current recommended version — there is no v4.0 release as of February 2026. The `cve-canary` and `json-sqli-canary` rules have no stable variant and must stay on canary.

The key technical change required is migrating rule expressions from the deprecated `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sqli-v33-stable')` to `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf('sqli-v33-stable', {'sensitivity': 1})`. The new function is required to control sensitivity levels and is the only one that inspects both request headers and body. The existing `tf-modules//waf` private module does not expose a `preconfigured_waf_config` variable, so per-service exclusions must either be expressed as CEL negation in the rule expression (no module change) or added as standalone `google_compute_security_policy_rule` resources outside the module (requires extending module interface).

**Core technologies:**
- `Terraform ~> 1.14`: IaC orchestration — already in use, no change required
- `Google Provider ~> 7.0`: GCP resource management — already in use; fully supports all WAF resources
- `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf()`: Rule expression function — replaces deprecated `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr()`; required for sensitivity control and body inspection
- `google_compute_security_policy_rule` with `preconfigured_waf_config`: Per-rule exclusion blocks — needed for Keycloak, Superset, Django admin
- `terraform_remote_state` (workspace: sec): Cross-module data source — propagates policy names from `sec/waf` to consumer LB modules

### Expected Features

**Must have (table stakes — required for QA milestone):**
- Fix rule 1020 bug (action contradicts description — currently blocks Stackdriver uptime checks)
- Migrate all rules from `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr()` to `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf()` with explicit `sensitivity: 1`
- Enable verbose logging (`log_level = VERBOSE`) on the WAF policy
- Deploy WAF policies in same-project as LBs using multi-provider in `sec/waf`
- Attach policy to `apps/gke`, `apps/frontends`, `apps/apps`, `apps/airflow` LBs (qa workspace, preview mode only)
- Establish Cloud Logging queries for preview-deny analysis
- Add `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusions for Keycloak before any session fixation or XSS rule activation
- Add `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusions for Superset/Metabase before any SQLi rule activation

**Should have (before marking milestone complete):**
- Django admin CSRF token exclusions (support-administration, backoffice-api)
- File upload endpoint exclusions (excel-loader, lms-excel-loader LFI/RFI)
- Kong API gateway method enforcement exclusion or rule disable
- Attach remaining LBs: `common/apps`, `bi/apps`, `bi/wrenai-poc`
- Cloud Monitoring alert for preview-deny rate spike (>5% of traffic)

**Defer to v2+ (post-QA validation):**
- Promote rules from preview to enforce (incremental, lowest-risk first)
- Rate limit differentiation per service tier (auth vs API vs static)
- Staging and production workspace rollout
- Adaptive Protection (separate billing tier)
- Upgrade to v33-canary CRS versions

### Architecture Approach

The architecture centers on `sec/waf` as the single source of truth for all WAF policies, using Terraform multi-provider aliases to deploy identical-base policies into each target GCP project from one state file (workspace: `sec`). Consumer LB modules (`apps/gke`, `apps/frontends`, etc.) add a `terraform_remote_state` data source pointing to `sec/waf` (workspace: `sec`) and pass the policy name to the existing `cloud_armor_policy` parameter. Since each policy lives in the same project as its LB, no cross-project IAM is required. Per-environment variations (different IP whitelists, BI tool SQL exclusions) are expressed in `sec/waf/locals.tf` as rule set overrides using `merge()`. WAF exclusion logic stays in `sec/waf` — consumer modules never contain WAF-specific logic.

**Major components:**
1. `sec/waf` — WAF policy definitions, multi-provider deployment, rule set management; owns all security decisions
2. `tf-modules//waf` — Private module creating `google_compute_security_policy` + rules; unchanged interface
3. `tf-modules//load-balancer` — Already accepts `cloud_armor_policy` string; no interface change required
4. LB consumer modules (7 modules) — Add `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source + wire `cloud_armor_policy`; minimal change per module
5. Cloud Logging / Cloud Monitoring — Analysis layer for preview-deny data; informs all exclusion decisions

### Critical Pitfalls

1. **Cross-project policy attachment silently fails** — A `google_compute_backend_service` in `qa-apps-454414` will reject a policy self_link from `security-454414`; requires Cloud Armor Enterprise to work. Avoid by deploying policies in each target project using `sec/waf` multi-provider aliases.

2. **Method enforcement (rule 1080) blocks all REST traffic** — OWASP CRS allows only GET/HEAD/POST/OPTIONS by default; PUT/PATCH/DELETE return 403. Every microservice uses REST conventions. Disable or globally exclude non-standard methods before any activation.

3. **Superset and Metabase are 100% broken by SQLi rules** — SQL query builder tools send legitimate SQL in POST bodies; no sensitivity level avoids this. Add path exclusions for `/api/` on the bi-apps LB policy before any SQLi rule activation.

4. **Logging is disabled by default** — `google_compute_backend_service` `log_config` is off unless explicitly set. Attaching WAF without enabling logging produces zero visibility. Enable `log_config { enable = true, sample_rate = 1.0 }` in the same apply as policy attachment.

5. **Rule 1020 configuration bug** — Current `sec/waf/waf.tf` has `action = "deny(403)"` on the Stackdriver monitoring rule with description "Permitir GoogleStackdriverMonitoring-UptimeChecks". Fix action to `"allow"` or remove the rule before any LB attachment.

6. **Keycloak triggers multiple rules simultaneously** — JWT tokens, session cookies, and PKCE parameters trigger XSS, session fixation, and scanner detection rules. Keycloak is the auth gateway for the entire platform; a false positive here blocks all users. Requires comprehensive path exclusions before session fixation or XSS rule activation.

7. **Bulk rule activation is undebuggable** — Flipping all `preview = false` simultaneously makes it impossible to isolate which rule caused which error. Activate one rule (or logical group) per 24-hour window with explicit monitoring gates.

---

## Implications for Roadmap

Based on research, the following 4-phase structure is recommended. Each phase has clear entry criteria from the previous phase and a hard gate before proceeding.

### Phase 1: Foundation Fixes and Architecture Setup

**Rationale:** Three pre-conditions must be true before any policy attachment: (1) the architecture question (same-project vs cross-project) must be resolved, (2) the rule 1020 bug must be fixed, and (3) the `sec/waf` module must be restructured to deploy via multi-provider. Without these, any LB attachment either fails or operates with a known bug active.

**Delivers:**
- Rule 1020 corrected (`deny(403)` → `allow`)
- All rules migrated to `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf()` with `sensitivity: 1`
- `sec/waf/providers.tf` extended with aliases for qa/prod/sha/bi projects
- `sec/waf/waf.tf` refactored to one module call per target project
- `sec/waf/outputs.tf` exporting `{env}_policy_name` per project
- Terraform SA in `sec` granted `roles/compute.securityAdmin` in qa/prod/sha/bi projects
- Validated: test apply confirms policy attaches to one QA backend service and logs appear

**Avoids:** Cross-project attachment failure (Pitfall 1), rule 1020 outage (Pitfall 5), silent no-logging WAF (Pitfall 4)

**Research flag:** Standard patterns — no additional research needed. All architecture decisions are resolved.

---

### Phase 2: QA Policy Attachment and Preview Analysis

**Rationale:** With the architecture validated, attach the policy in preview mode to all QA LBs and enable verbose logging. This phase generates the log data required to make all exclusion decisions in Phase 3. No rule should leave preview mode during this phase.

**Delivers:**
- Verbose logging enabled on `sec/waf` policy (`log_level = VERBOSE`)
- `terraform_remote_state.waf` data source added to all 7 LB consumer modules
- `cloud_armor_policy` wired in: `apps/gke`, `apps/frontends`, `apps/apps`, `apps/airflow` (qa workspace)
- `cloud_armor_policy` wired in: `common/apps` (sha workspace), `bi/apps`, `bi/wrenai-poc` (bi workspace)
- All rules remain `preview = true`
- Backend service `log_config` enabled at `sample_rate = 1.0` on all attached services
- Cloud Logging queries documented for preview-deny analysis per LB

**Uses:** Remote state propagation pattern (Pattern 2 from ARCHITECTURE.md)

**Avoids:** Logging disabled pitfall (Pitfall 4), silent WAF with no visibility

**Research flag:** Standard patterns — well-documented Terraform remote state pattern already used in codebase (KMS, VPC, SSL). No additional research needed.

---

### Phase 3: Endpoint Analysis and Exclusion Configuration

**Rationale:** Preview logs from Phase 2 reveal which rules fire on which services. This phase systematically catalogues false positives and writes `preconfigured_waf_config` exclusions or CEL expression negations for each high-risk service. No rule goes active until its exclusion surface is confirmed clean in preview logs over a minimum 7-day window.

**Delivers:**
- False positive register documenting every preview-deny entry by service, rule, and field
- Method enforcement rule (1080) decision: disable for REST APIs or add per-method exclusions
- Keycloak exclusions: session fixation, XSS, scanner detection (covering `/auth/realms/*/` paths)
- Superset/Metabase SQLi exclusions: `/api/` path exclusions on bi-apps LB policy
- Django admin XSS/SQLi exclusions: `csrftoken` cookie, `x-csrftoken` header, `/admin/` paths
- File upload LFI/RFI exclusions: excel-loader and lms-excel-loader upload endpoint paths
- Kong method enforcement exclusion (if not globally disabled)
- Content-Length protection rule (>8KB to non-upload endpoints)
- Rate limit analysis: Cloud Scheduler source IP behavior in preview logs
- All exclusions confirmed via 7-day preview window with zero false positives per service

**Implements:** Per-environment exclusion strategy (Pattern 3 from ARCHITECTURE.md)

**Avoids:** Superset/Metabase SQLi breakage (Pitfall 3), Keycloak auth outage (Pitfall 4), REST method enforcement outage (Pitfall 2), file upload bypass gap (Pitfall 7), rate limit scheduler impact (Pitfall 6)

**Research flag:** May need deeper research per service. Keycloak exclusion patterns are MEDIUM confidence — specific rule IDs that fire must be confirmed from actual preview logs, not just assumed from documentation. Excel-loader exact upload paths must be confirmed from application routing. Rate limit behavior of Cloud Scheduler IPs needs empirical validation from logs.

---

### Phase 4: Incremental Rule Activation (Enforce Mode)

**Rationale:** With exclusions confirmed and preview logs clean, rules are activated one at a time in risk order from least to most impactful. Each activation has a 24-hour monitoring window before the next rule proceeds.

**Delivers:**
- Rules promoted to `preview = false` in this order:
  1. Scanner detection (1090) — lowest false positive rate
  2. LFI (1050), RFI (1070) — rarely triggered by legitimate REST traffic
  3. RCE (1060), Java (1130), NodeJS (1140) — focused signatures
  4. Protocol attacks (1100)
  5. XSS (1040) — after admin panel traffic confirmed clean
  6. Session fixation (1120) — only after Keycloak exclusions confirmed in production logs
  7. SQLi (1030), JSON-SQLi (1160) — only after BI tool exclusions confirmed
  8. Method enforcement (1080) — likely disabled for REST APIs; activate only if scoped carefully
  9. Rate limiting (1170) — activate last; Scheduler IP behavior must be validated first
- Verbose logging disabled after enforcement confirmed stable (PII/cost consideration)
- Cloud Monitoring alert configured for enforce-mode deny rate
- `sample_rate` reduced from 1.0 to 0.1 after tuning complete

**Avoids:** Bulk activation debugging nightmare (Pitfall 8), rate limit scheduler blocking (Pitfall 6)

**Research flag:** Standard — incremental activation is a documented best practice. The activation order is derived from official GCP Cloud Armor best practices documentation. No additional research needed.

---

### Phase 5: Staging and Production Rollout (Future Milestone)

**Rationale:** After QA enforcement is stable for 30+ days, replicate the same policy attachment and exclusion configuration to staging and production workspaces. Production rollout requires independent log analysis since traffic patterns differ.

**Delivers:**
- Staging workspace policy attachment and preview period
- Production workspace policy attachment and preview period
- Per-workspace exclusion tuning based on production traffic patterns

**Note:** This is a separate future milestone. The current milestone scope ends at Phase 4 (QA enforcement).

**Research flag:** No additional research needed — patterns established in Phases 1-4 apply directly.

---

### Phase Ordering Rationale

- Phase 1 must precede all others: the architecture question blocks all downstream work, and the rule bug must be fixed before any attachment
- Phase 2 cannot be parallelized with Phase 1: policy must be deployed before LBs can attach
- Phase 3 is entirely dependent on log data from Phase 2: exclusions cannot be written without knowing which fields trigger which rules
- Phase 4 is gated on Phase 3 being clean: no rule should ever go active without confirmed zero false positives
- The 7-day minimum preview window in Phase 3 is the longest constraint; plan the timeline accordingly
- Kong activation must be last within Phase 4: Kong proxies all downstream services, so a false positive there breaks the entire platform

### Research Flags

Phases requiring deeper research during planning:
- **Phase 3:** Service-specific exclusion patterns are MEDIUM confidence. Keycloak session fixation exclusions, Django CSRF cookie exclusion behavior, and exact upload paths for excel-loader require validation from actual preview log data before finalizing Terraform configuration.
- **Phase 3:** Cloud Scheduler source IP behavior under rate limiting is empirically unknown for this infrastructure. The IP ranges are not static and cannot be pre-whitelisted. Requires 48-hour preview window analysis specifically targeting rule 1170 before any conclusion.

Phases with standard patterns (skip additional research):
- **Phase 1:** Multi-provider Terraform pattern is well-documented. IAM grant process is standard GCP. Rule expression migration is a one-line change per rule.
- **Phase 2:** Remote state propagation pattern already used in 10+ modules in this codebase.
- **Phase 4:** Incremental activation sequence is explicitly recommended in GCP Cloud Armor best practices documentation.

---

## Confidence Assessment

| Area | Confidence | Notes |
|------|------------|-------|
| Stack | HIGH | Official GCP docs + direct codebase inspection. No ambiguity on versions, resource types, or expression syntax. |
| Features | HIGH | Table stakes features are well-established WAF deployment patterns. Service-specific exclusion patterns are MEDIUM for exact field/path configurations — these require log validation. |
| Architecture | HIGH | Cross-project policy constraint confirmed via multiple official GCP sources. Multi-provider pattern is well-documented Terraform behavior. Remote state pattern is already proven in this codebase. |
| Pitfalls | HIGH | Critical pitfalls (rule 1020 bug, method enforcement, Superset SQLi) confirmed via direct code inspection. Cross-project limitation confirmed via official docs. Keycloak and scheduler pitfalls are MEDIUM — based on community patterns and documented behavior, but exact exclusion configurations require empirical validation. |

**Overall confidence:** HIGH

### Gaps to Address

- **Cross-project attachment final validation:** ARCHITECTURE.md confirms the mechanism is invalid without Enterprise, and STACK.md agrees. The multi-provider pattern is the recommended solution. However, a minimal test apply to one QA backend service during Phase 1 should be done before committing the full multi-provider refactor — to confirm the same-project policy attachment works correctly via remote state output.

- **Exact Keycloak exclusion rule IDs:** The session fixation and XSS rules that fire on Keycloak traffic are identified (1120, 1040), but the specific OWASP CRS signature IDs (e.g., `owasp-crs-v030301-id943110`) must be read from actual preview logs. The exclusion config templates in FEATURES.md are correct patterns but need real `matchedFieldType`/`matchedFieldValue` data to be finalized.

- **Excel-loader upload endpoint path:** FEATURES.md shows `/main/upload` as the assumed path. This must be confirmed from the application's routing configuration before writing the LFI/RFI exclusion rule. An incorrect path means the exclusion does nothing and the service remains blocked.

- **Rate limit threshold adequacy:** 1000 req/min per IP has not been validated against actual traffic metrics for the highest-volume services (tms-api, tracking-service, kong). This should be validated against Cloud Monitoring historical metrics before Phase 4 rate limit activation.

- **`tf-modules//waf` module interface for `preconfigured_waf_config`:** The private module does not expose this block. Two approaches are documented: (A) CEL expression negation within the existing `expr` field — no module change, (B) standalone `google_compute_security_policy_rule` resources outside the module. The CEL approach is preferred for this milestone to avoid private module changes, but its limitations (no per-field operator support) must be acceptable for the required exclusions.

---

## Sources

### Primary (HIGH confidence)
- [Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/waf-rules) — Rule set names, CRS versions, evaluatePreconfiguredWaf syntax
- [Tune Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/rule-tuning) — Sensitivity levels, opt_out/opt_in, exclusion block structure
- [Cloud Armor rules language reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/rules-language-reference) — evaluatePreconfiguredExpr deprecation, evaluatePreconfiguredWaf signature
- [Cloud Armor Enterprise overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/armor-enterprise-overview) — Cross-project referencing requires Enterprise enrollment
- [Configure Cloud Armor security policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/configure-security-policies) — Attachment mechanics and scope
- [Cloud Armor best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/best-practices) — Preview mode strategy, incremental activation
- [Cloud Armor request logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/request-logging) — Log fields, preview vs enforce log distinction, logging disabled by default
- [Cloud Armor verbose logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/verbose-logging) — Available log fields, privacy considerations
- [Terraform google_compute_security_policy](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-google/blob/main/website/docs/r/compute_security_policy.html.markdown) — Resource attributes, preconfigured_waf_config schema
- Direct codebase inspection: `sec/waf/waf.tf`, `sec/waf/.terraform/modules/`, `apps/gke/load-balancer.tf`, `bi/apps/remote-state.tf` — current implementation and gaps

### Secondary (MEDIUM confidence)
- [Cloud Armor method enforcement discussion](https://discuss.google.dev/t/cloud-armor-method-enforcement-additional-http-methods/141698) — REST API method blocking behavior
- [Keycloak WAF CRS compatibility discussion](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/discussions/35586) — Session fixation and XSS false positive patterns
- [Metabase WAF SQLi bypass discussion](https://discourse.metabase.com/t/bypass-metabase-apis-from-wafs-for-sql-injection/24769) — SQL query builder false positive patterns
- [Cloud Armor hierarchical security policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/hierarchical-policies-using) — Org/folder-level policies as alternative to per-project

### Tertiary (LOW confidence, needs validation)
- [8KB WAF inspection limit guide](https://kloudle.com/academy/a-guide-to-protect-against-the-8kb-waf-limitation-in-google-cloud-armor/) — File upload bypass risk
- Cross-project Cloud Armor Standard (non-Enterprise) attachment feasibility — official docs ambiguous; confirmed invalid via architecture research but warrants a single test apply

---

## SYNTHESIS COMPLETE

**Files synthesized:**

### Executive Summary

Cloud Armor WAF activation for the Liftit multi-project GCP infrastructure requires a 4-phase approach: (1) fix pre-existing bugs and refactor `sec/waf` to use Terraform multi-provider aliases to deploy same-project policies, (2) attach policies to all LBs in preview mode with verbose logging, (3) analyze preview logs to build per-service exclusions before any enforcement, (4) activate rules incrementally one at a time. The architecturally critical constraint — that Cloud Armor policies cannot be shared cross-project without Cloud Armor Enterprise — means the intended centralized-in-sec architecture is invalid and must be replaced with per-project policy deployment from a single `sec/waf` state.

# Requirements: Cloud Armor WAF Implementation

**Defined:** 2026-02-24
**Core Value:** Protect all externally-exposed services from OWASP attacks and abuse without blocking legitimate traffic.

## v1 Requirements

Requirements for QA environment rollout. Each maps to roadmap phases.

### Endpoint Analysis

- [ ] **AUDIT-01**: All 35+ GKE microservices analyzed for HTTP methods, payload patterns, and WAF-sensitive content (SQL-like input, file uploads, encoded tokens)
- [ ] **AUDIT-02**: VM-based apps analyzed (n8n/workflows, kutt/urlshortener, OSRM, inventarios, airflow, metabase, superset, wrenai, streamlit, sonar, monitor)
- [ ] **AUDIT-03**: High-risk services identified with specific WAF rules that will trigger false positives (Keycloak, Kong, backoffice, Superset, Metabase, excel-loaders, docscan, support-admin)
- [ ] **AUDIT-04**: False positive risk matrix created per service per WAF rule (which rules affect which services)
- [ ] **AUDIT-05**: Preview mode logs analyzed in QA for 7+ days to validate static analysis findings with actual traffic

### WAF Infrastructure

- [ ] **WAF-01**: Rule 1020 bug fixed (action contradicts description — blocking uptime checks instead of allowing)
- [ ] **WAF-02**: All 15 preconfigured OWASP rules migrated from `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr()` to `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf()` with sensitivity level 1
- [ ] **WAF-03**: sec/waf module refactored to deploy policies into each target project via Terraform multi-provider aliases (qa, prod, sha, bi)
- [ ] **WAF-04**: IAM bindings configured for sec Terraform SA to manage Cloud Armor policies in qa, prod, sha, bi projects (`roles/compute.securityAdmin`)
- [ ] **WAF-05**: sec/waf outputs updated to expose policy name per project for remote state consumption
- [ ] **WAF-06**: Verbose logging enabled on WAF policy for preview analysis

### Policy Attachment

- [ ] **ATTACH-01**: WAF policy attached to GKE LB in QA (`apps/gke`, workspace qa) via remote state from sec/waf
- [ ] **ATTACH-02**: WAF policy attached to Airflow LB in QA (`apps/airflow`, workspace qa)
- [ ] **ATTACH-03**: WAF policy attached to Apps LB in QA (`apps/apps`, workspace qa — n8n/workflows, inventarios)
- [ ] **ATTACH-04**: WAF policy attached to Shared Apps LB (`common/apps`, workspace sha — kutt, sonar, OSRM, monitor)
- [ ] **ATTACH-05**: WAF policy attached to BI Apps LB (`bi/apps`, workspace bi — metabase, superset)
- [ ] **ATTACH-06**: WAF policy attached to WrenAI LB (`bi/wrenai-poc`, workspace bi — wrenai, streamlit)

### Exclusion Configuration

- [ ] **EXCL-01**: SQLi exclusions configured for Superset and Metabase (API paths that send SQL in POST bodies)
- [ ] **EXCL-02**: Method enforcement exclusions configured for services using PUT/DELETE/PATCH (all microservices, Kong)
- [ ] **EXCL-03**: Keycloak-specific exclusions configured (auth flows, session tokens, SAML/OIDC payloads)
- [ ] **EXCL-04**: File upload service exclusions configured (excel-loader, lms-excel-loader, docscan-service) for LFI/RFI rules
- [ ] **EXCL-05**: Django admin exclusions configured (support-administration, backoffice-api) for XSS/CSRF patterns
- [ ] **EXCL-06**: Cloud Scheduler IP ranges whitelisted or excluded from rate limiting rule

### Rule Activation

- [ ] **ACTIV-01**: Rules activated incrementally one at a time with 24-hour monitoring gates between each activation
- [ ] **ACTIV-02**: IP whitelist rule (1000) validated as active and correct per workspace
- [ ] **ACTIV-03**: All OWASP preconfigured rules (1030-1160) transitioned from preview to active in QA after exclusion validation
- [ ] **ACTIV-04**: Rate limiting rule (1170) activated after threshold validation against actual QA traffic patterns
- [ ] **ACTIV-05**: User-agent blocking rule (1010) activated after validating no legitimate bots are blocked
- [ ] **ACTIV-06**: Zero false positives confirmed in QA for 48+ hours after full activation

### Documentation

- [ ] **DOCS-01**: WAF operations runbook created (how to review logs, add exclusions, temporarily disable a rule, respond to false positive reports)
- [ ] **DOCS-02**: Service-to-rule mapping documented (which services have which exclusions and why)
- [ ] **DOCS-03**: CLAUDE.md for sec/waf updated with new multi-provider architecture and cross-project pattern

## v2 Requirements

Deferred to future milestone. Tracked but not in current roadmap.

### Staging/Production Rollout

- **ROLLOUT-01**: Replicate QA WAF attachment to staging environment
- **ROLLOUT-02**: Replicate QA WAF attachment to production environment
- **ROLLOUT-03**: Production-specific rate limiting thresholds tuned to actual traffic

### Advanced Protection

- **ADV-01**: Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection evaluated and configured
- **ADV-02**: Preconfigured rule versions upgraded from v33-stable to latest
- **ADV-03**: Custom WAF rules for Liftit-specific attack patterns
- **ADV-04**: Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerts for WAF events

### Frontend Protection

- **FRONT-01**: Alternative protection for GCS frontend static sites (Cloudflare WAF or Edge Security Policy)

## Out of Scope

| Feature | Reason |
|---------|--------|
| Cloud Armor Enterprise | $3k/month; per-project multi-provider deployment achieves same result |
| Cross-project centralized policy | Requires Enterprise tier; multi-provider aliases solve this |

| Frontend WAF (GCS buckets) | GCP limitation: backend_bucket does not support security_policy |
| Upgrading to newer rule versions | Focus on activating v33-stable first; upgrade in v2 |

1→# Cloud Armor WAF Implementation
     2→
     3→## What This Is
     4→
     5→Implementation of Google Cloud Armor WAF policies across the Liftit GCP infrastructure. Centralizes a single WAF security policy in the `sec` project (security-454414) and attaches it to all 7 load balancers across environments, starting with QA. Includes endpoint analysis to prevent false positives before activation.
     6→
     7→## Core Value
     8→
     9→Protect all externally-exposed services from OWASP attacks and abuse without blocking legitimate traffic.
    10→
    11→## Current Milestone: v1.0 Cloud Armor QA Rollout
    12→
    13→**Goal:** Analyze all services behind load balancers, fine-tune WAF rules to prevent false positives, centralize the policy in sec, and attach it to QA load balancers.
    14→
    15→**Target features:**
    16→- Audit all services behind LBs for WAF compatibility (endpoints, payloads, patterns)
    17→- Centralize WAF policy in sec project (single policy shared across all projects)
    18→- Fine-tune WAF rules based on endpoint analysis (exclusions, sensitivity tuning)
    19→- Attach WAF policy to all QA load balancers
    20→- Transition rules from preview to active after validation
    21→

    23→
    24→### Validated
    25→
    26→<!-- Shipped and confirmed valuable. -->
    27→
    28→- WAF policy module exists (`sec/waf/`) with 18 rules using preconfigured OWASP rule sets
    29→- All 7 load balancers support `cloud_armor_policy` parameter (currently `null`)
    30→- WAF module in tf-modules supports rules, rate limiting, and IP whitelisting
    31→
    32→### Active
    33→
    34→<!-- Current scope. Building toward these. -->

    41→- [ ] Attach WAF policy to all 7 QA load balancers
    42→- [ ] Validate no false positives in QA
    43→
    44→### Out of Scope
    45→
    46→<!-- Explicit boundaries. Includes reasoning to prevent re-adding. -->
    47→
    48→- Upgrading preconfigured rule versions (v33-stable to newer) — separate milestone after QA validation

    53→

    61→

    65→
    66→**Load balancers to protect (7 total):**
    67→| Module | LB Name | Backend Type | Services | Workspace |
    68→|--------|---------|-------------|----------|-----------|
    69→| apps/gke | gke-apps | Zonal NEG | 35+ microservices | qa/staging/prod |
    70→| apps/frontends | frontends | Backend bucket | 14+ static sites | qa/staging/prod |
    71→| apps/airflow | airflow | Instance group | Airflow VM | qa/prod |
    72→| apps/apps | apps-{ws} | Instance group | n8n, inventarios | qa/prod |
    73→| common/apps | sha-apps | Instance group | kutt, sonar, OSRM, monitor | sha |
    74→| bi/apps | bi-apps | Instance group | Metabase, Superset | bi |
    75→| bi/wrenai-poc | wrenai-poc | Instance group | WrenAI, Streamlit | bi |
